title: Get swept up in the nostalgia and enjoy it... just don't think too hard about it.
review:
OK so I went into TFA with very low expectations, mostly because it was directed by JJ Abrams and he single-handedly slaughtered the Star Trek timeline with his two horrendous movies (don't get me started on that we'll be here all day).

So I was pleasantly surprised at the beginning of this film that it actually felt like a Star Wars film. From the opening credits to the storm troopers and ship designs it gave me that warm and fuzzy nostalgic feeling from my childhood which pretty much carried me throughout the movie and let me walking out of the cinema having thoroughly enjoyed it.

However when the nostalgic feeling eventually dissipated and I actually thought about the content of the movie there were so many plot holes it was ridiculous (I've actually seen a blog where someone has collated a total of 40 plot holes in total. Google it, it's impressive).

SPOILERS AHEAD! You have been warned!

As so many have before me have pointed out I can't start this review without acknowledging that it was a blatant re-hashing of Episode IV. And through my nostalgic delirium JJ managed to avoid me noticing this until the moment in the command centre when they discussed how to destroy the Star Killer (and in particular how to disable the shield). Yeah we noticed JJ.

Oh and FYI once you take all the fuel from a sun it burns out and there's no sunlight any more. It doesn't just magically re-ignite itself.

Overall everything was too convenient to the point that I roll my eyes now just thinking about it. The best example being that Han and Chewy just HAPPENED to be near Jakku at the same time Rey and Finn flew the Millennium Falcon off the planet in god knows how many years? Riiiiight.

So in order to truly articulate all of my feelings about this movie I shall break it down by character:

Leia: No disrespect to Carrie Fisher but she couldn't act in 1983 and she clearly hasn't taken any acting classes in the last 22 years because she still can't act. Her only saving grace is that her most important scene was with Harrison Ford and he made her look really really good. Also what qualifies her to be a General when she's not completed any military service?

Han Solo: Yep Harrison Ford pretty much makes this movie watchable. Let's face it, a cantankerous, sarcastic Han Solo is funny. Also unlike some people who have reviewed on this site I totally buy the whole going-back-to-being-a-smuggler-even-though-he's-well-past-his-prime- as-a-way-to-deal-with-his-son-going- Dark-Side thing. A lot of the times when we're in emotional turmoil we like to run away to a point in our lives where everything was good. And finally he deserved a much better death than what he got quite frankly. He just stands there while his son guts him with a light saber? And what the hell were Chewy, Ren and Finn doing just watching it happen?!

Kylo Ren: Yeah don't make a petulant 20-something-year-old with major daddy issues the bad guy of your movie. And if you are going to do that, DON'T LET HIM TAKE OFF THE BADASS LOOKING HELMET.

Rey: I liked Daisy Ridley's performance a lot. My criticisms about her character are not a reflection of her acting, but of the writing. Making the female character instantly an expert at flying the Millennium Falcon was just laziness. Oh and even though she had never heard of the Force and believed it was a myth before this little adventure she instinctively knows that she can manipulate weaker minds to release her from her shackles and successfully carry on a light saber fight with her cousin (who has actually trained as a Jedi). Ugh!

Finn: Oh where do I begin? A storm trooper who was kidnapped as a child, raised by the First Order and then on his first mission he freaks out and releases a prisoner to escape? And for some reason it seems like this is the first time this has ever happened in 30 years + but the First Order don't seem all that concerned about it? And for someone who's been indoctrinated by the First Order for most of his life he's social skills are remarkably well developed. And don't even get me started on how convenient it is that he knows everything about the Star Killer even though he worked in sanitation and how to shoot blasters on the Millennium Falcon like he's been doing it all his life. And finally YOU'RE NOT A JEDI SO PUT THE DAMN LIGHTSABER DOWN. Not cool man. Not cool.

Poe: I like Poe a lot. Although I thought it was rather convenient that when the fighter crashed into Jakkhu and he was thrown free from the crash his jacket was left behind? How did that happen I wonder?

Snoke: Yeah if you're going to rip off a bad guy from another sci-fi movie don't make it a cross between Gollum from LOTR and Parallax from "Green Lantern". Enough said.

Captain Phasma: WHAT WAS THE POINT OF A HAVING A BADASS FEMALE STORM TROOPER CAPTAIN WHEN AT THE FIRST SIGN OF CAPTURE SHE JUST DOES WHATEVER HER HOST TAKERS WANT??

I could go on and on and on but I should get back to work now.

Last word: Entertaining with a few laughs but plot holes big enough to fly the original Death Star through.

title: Weak effort relying on endless battles in absence of character and plot
review:
First: I have been a Star Wars fan since the early 1980s. I LOVE Star Wars. By the time Return of the Jedi came round, I could feel a disturbance in the Force, and the Sith plan to destroy the magic of New Hope and Empire Strikes Back was fully enacted by Phantom Menace et al.

Now to The Force Awakens. Clearly some effort has been made to recapture the look and feel of New Hope, but no effort whatsoever given to plot, dialogue or character development. The film is MINDLESS. Huge, gaping plot holes are filled with endless laser battles, no doubt designed to sell the console games that will follow. After seeing Awakens at the cinema, I returned home disheartened. I watched New Hope again and can say that on all counts it is a far, far better film. It has a tight storyline, good characters, plenty of humour, the action zips along without getting boring. We all KNOW what a good film New Hope is.

Now to the SPOILERS (though not major ones) - what is so bad about this film? Here we go:

1. The PLOT. Droid carrying data vital to the rebellion lands on a desert planet and is found by a descendant (no doubt) of Anakin Skywalker who doesn't realise they are strong with the Force. There is a chase by Imperial troops (OK, "First Order" troops) lead by a Sith knight wearing a black helmet and cloak and carrying a red lightsaber. The young Jedi-to-be escapes in the Millennium Falcon. The Empire (OK, "First Order") have built a planet-sized weapon which fires an energy beam capable of destroying planets, which they demonstrate. The Rebellion attacks this with small fighters but to do this a small groups has to land and de-activate shields or whatever. A lovable father-figure character is killed by the guy in black with the red light sabre. The young Jedi-to-be has to fly to a remote system to meet a Jedi master. DOES ANY OF THIS SOUND FAMILIAR? So, they couldn't be bothered to write a new, interesting story. Just dig out the old.

2. The CHARACTERS. We met a series of one-dimensional characters (a clichéd fighter pilot, a shouty Nazi ginger-haired general, a wise old woman who's only purpose was to hand over an old lightsaber). The new Darth Vader impersonator had the old daddy- issues but in reverse. Poor old Max von Sydow (one of my favourite actors) got just enough screen time to MacGuffin the plot along. Only Chewbacca got any kind of character development. Finn was pretty good but utterly unbelievable - someone raised from birth to be a mindless stormtrooper suddenly develops a full character and a sense of humour?? Ren is a beautiful woman but utterly unconvincing - a top engineer as well as learning various Force tricks by herself within a few days. There was no subtlety to be found anywhere.

3. PLOT HOLES and MACGUFFINS. How could a fully formed New Empire arise, and build a weapon of that size, within 30 years, completely undetected by the Republic? OK, space is big as they say, but surely someone would have seen something? Why would a Jedi Master leave a map to his whereabouts if he clearly doesn't want to be found? Why would a certain lightsaber be found in a convenient box kept by an old lady (who conveniently dismisses this by saying 'its a long story' - well tell us, we're here for 2 hours and we're bored of spaceship battles!). I haven't really been aware of MacGuffins before (unexplained characters or events that move the plot along) but this film is full to the rafters with them.

This film is lazy, lazy writing in the extreme. Still, its what the kids want these days and the money is rolling in, so who am I to argue. My time was the 80s when the films were fresh and exciting. These days, it seems, any old junk will do.

I rather naively supposed that the deficiencies of the prequels would lend some insight into what was needed for any further movies that might be made. The funny thing is it didn't work out that way. If anything TFA highlights some of the few things the prequels handled better, such as the score, the bigger sense of scale, Darth Maul and dare I say it greater imagination overall. The major flaw they share in common is bad execution of certain specifics.In prequels case pacing, shitty dialogue, character motivation and general lack of finesse during the key moments. In the case of TFA all its specific faults are in danger of coming of the rails because of the manic pace of the film. There needs to be moments of pause and slower pacing at key moments. I won't fault the actors in either set of films, any deficiencies were due in my opinion to characterization and dialogue. I have seen many of the actors in other roles which have been handled well. If you want to make a believable female lead then take a look at Sarah Connor and Ellen Ripley, believable, fleshed out and yes STRONG. Finn was a wasted opportunity. The trailer hinted at more than comic relief. Perhaps Kylo could have been worked if a little more care was spent on making him work. The cheap coincidences I do not need to mention as others out there have eyes to see what is obvious.What does this mean for the future of the franchise? I would hope that episode 8 redeems this mess because if it doesn't I won't bother again. I will give this movie a 4 because it would be ridiculous to go much lower than that as I have seen worse. title: The Force Reawakens
review:
Over the long wait for Star Wars: the Force Awakens, one question has been omnipresent: would a Star Wars film made without the involvement of series creator George Lucas improve on the controversial prequels? Or would it be what we feared most - not so much a real installment, as a marketing tool for selling action figures and LEGOs? As much as we had hoped otherwise, we now must face the truth: even when making Star Wars movies, Disney will be Disney.

Quite simply, The Force Awakens fails to pass the main test of a good sequel - that it have something to add to the story. While we need not believe that Luke, Han, and Leia simply danced with Ewoks for the rest of their lives, couldn't J.J. Abrams have found a better way to continue the Star Wars saga than to reset its every development so that it could be done all over again? In retelling A New Hope, he has not only created a boring film, but has obliterated the original story: the Empire has completely returned; Han is once again a self-centered rogue, a famous romance is destroyed; and Luke is less than we've ever seen him, a coward hiding from his problems. Thanks, Disney. Now, my kids can think the original Star Wars Trilogy was the tale of a bunch of losers who never defeated an Empire, and was totally superfluous to the overall story arc of the Star Wars saga.

As if it weren't enough that the story is a total rehash, it has a plot hole you could fly a Star Destroyer through: the existence of the map to Luke. Who created it? How did the pieces get scattered in a bunch of wildly different places? None of the characters act as if there's a mystery here; it's as though we're meant to take the map's existence for granted. Or are we supposed to assume that Luke tried to explain his location in a Blues Clues-type fashion, hiding puzzle pieces about the galaxy instead of just telling people?

Throughout the film, Abrams rushes from scene to scene without genuine character development or exposition. How can we care about the main character, Rey, when the only thing she ever expresses any real interest in is being home... when she expresses any emotions at all? Also, the relationship of the two leads is underdeveloped and confined mostly to the realm of comic relief. The pace never slows even to honor the death - and a most un-heroic and unfitting one at that - of a certain major character; there's no eulogy, no funeral; not even a word spoken of it. With everything Abrams once borrowed from Star Trek II, he couldn't take a cue from that film now?

The film has little to contribute to the Star Wars universe. It is set thirty years after Return of the Jedi, but the physical appearance of its world hasn't changed, except for the addition of a spherical droid and a three-bladed lightsaber. It's not just that it's lazy; it's that from an in-universe perspective, it makes no sense that so little innovation has occurred in thirty years when between Episodes III and IV it happened dramatically in a much shorter time. The locations are nearly identical to ones from the Original Trilogy. It's Tatooine; why even bother calling it Jakku? All of it complements the already overwhelming feeling of sameness.

As far as style and craftsmanship are concerned, this is at best a superficial imitation of earlier Star Wars films. The circle transitions are still here, but little else is. The previous films were masterfully crafted works of art. There was thought behind each camera angle. There were interesting set pieces for the lightsaber duels. There was the presence of suspense, as with Vader's first entrance, or the Falcon being pulled into the Death Star. Here, everything is about explosions and lightsaber-waving.

Perhaps the worst part of it all is that Abrams has nothing to say. For a film that has "Force" in the title, there's little actual talk of it. Neither does the film contain any allegory, any philosophy, any moral depth, or one small nugget of wisdom.

There are some positives to the film - namely, far better acting and scriptwriting than the prequels, and more vivid characterizations. Although the script doesn't have the memorable, quotable nature of the Original Trilogy ones, it's laced with plenty of amusing quips. But important though these elements are, they can't save a film from a through-and-through bad story.

Whatever merits The Force Awakens does possess, nothing can change the fact that it is, deep down, disingenuous and false. The best I can say of it is that it has given me a newfound great appreciation for George Lucas' deeply flawed, but heartfelt and genuinely moving prequels, which are the superior of this film in so many respects: story, character development, emotion, depth, artfulness, and world-building. It has highlighted the inescapable genius of his vision for Star Wars, a genius which has no place near Disney's soulless assembly line movie-making. We're sorry, George, for our criticism; everything is forgiven. Because if we've learned anything from The Force Awakens, it's that Star Wars is lost without its creator at the helm.

Reused Plot Elements:

  • Empire attacks Rebels in search of plot device containing important information. Character hides plot device in cute droid, before being kidnapped. (IV)


  • Droid is purchased from scrap dealers by the protagonist, an orphan who lives on a desert planet. (IV)


  • Main characters escape desert planet in Millennium Falcon, pursued by Storm Troopers, before Falcon is sucked inside larger spacecraft. (IV)


  • Han Solo is a smuggler who lives for himself, but later realizes the importance of fighting for the common good. When he is first introduced, he becomes involved in a violent confrontation over his debts. (IV)


  • Leia initially behaves coldly towards Han, but later reveals affection for him. (V)


  • Main characters enter a cantina in search of transportation. (IV)


  • Empire kidnaps girl and interrogates her to obtain the plot device, and girl must be rescued. (IV)


  • Father/son, light/dark conflict, in which a character thinks he can turn his Sith family member back to the light. (VI)


  • During the mission to rescue the girl, the character who serves as a mentor to the other main characters confronts the villain, a person he used to have a close relationship with years ago, and is killed. (IV)


  • A planet-shaped superweapon is destroyed by flying into trenches (IV) and disabling a shield generator. (VI)


  • The protagonist seeks out a Jedi Master living in seclusion on a lonely planet, (V) who hides there because of a failure that allowed the Dark Side to rise to power. (III)

  • Protagonist who starts out on a desert planet, doesn't know her parents, and (if Luke's monologue in teaser #2 is any clue) has some family relationship to the main villain. (IV-V)

title: Some title suggestions for the re-release of TFA in special edition in 2050 that will undoubtedly make billions
review:
1) Finding Nemo meets Despicable Me meets A New Hope:

Nemo= Luke, Steve Carell= Kylo Ren (I want to be the most evil villain EVER!), A New Hope= the plot for this movie.

2) Darth Millennial and the failure of liberal parenting:

Harrison Ford was a cool, fun dad, who raised his kid on good California values of jedi training and organic food. But Kylo Ren just wanted to be a Republican like grandpa.

And though I thought this whole family drama felt incredibly fake and contrived, maybe subconsciously it's a critique of American family life. Maybe it's saying that if we keep raising our children the way we do, they're going to all end up as bad guys- and not cool, scary bad guys, like Darth Vader, but pathetic, disappointing ones...

Anyways, it's a long shot, but I'm just trying to find some deep meaning in this very not-deep movie...

3) Star Wars Episode VII: How to get rich without even trying... to write a plot.

Here's how I think TFA was made: market research was done to find everyone's favorite parts of episodes IV and V (not VI because it received the worst reviews out of the original trilogy). Then a computer was used to randomly organize the data into a film that a 4th Grader could sit through. (snow on Hoth- we'll put that on the new Death Star, Han Solo being a fun smuggler- we'll reset his character development to pre-episode IV, storm troopers- we'll just bring those back, etc.)

4) Star Wars Episode VII: How to marry your mother, kill your father, and make a ton of money.

So Star Wars has a few family themes: the good son rebelling against the evil father (Luke and Vader), the emo son rebelling against his cool father (Kylo Ren and Harrison Ford), and finally, the business savvy son (Abrams) rebelling against his out of touch father (Lucas) and marrying his rich mother (Disney), to the delight of the masses.

5) Star Wars Episode VII: attack of the horribly named bad guys:

The First Order? Supreme Leader Snoke? The Starkiller Base? Heaven help us all, sounds like the cartoon names guy scored a side gig with TFA and didn't get paid very much of that $200 million.

6) Star Wars Episode VII: The explosions are fun, the nostalgia is real, and the force is definitely asleep.

I've been pretty negative, but there were a few things I enjoyed about TFA. Here's a couple:

  • When the Millennium Falcon is introduced as "that piece of junk." The perfect appeal to my nostalgia, nice work J.J.


  • The fact that one of the heroes is a Storm Trooper- an interesting idea, that could have led to a lot of interesting moral discussion (but didn't).


  • Daisy Ridley's performance- she just felt like she fit in Star Wars, nice casting.


It was an entertaining movie, and it didn't have any particularly painful moments. But it didn't have any particularly "real" moments either, and by the end I was completely uninvested in the characters and the plot. Rather than having genuinely interesting central conflict, it simply used obvious artificial dangers to fill in the gaps. Like:

-That pilot guy disappearing. Obviously not dead.

-Fin leaving Rey to go off on his own. Obviously not going to happen.

-Han Solo not going to join in the fight against the Empire, but do his own thing instead. Seriously, we're doing this again?

Instead of there being an overarching plot, the writers- and the characters- were constantly running from the emptiness of this recycled "blow up the Death Star" story. The "peril of the moment" was used to try to hide the fact that no one actually knew what the "greater peril" was, because this new world with these new bad guys who looked surprisingly familiar is not at all organized or well thought-out.

7) Star Wars Episode VII: You either die a hero or live long enough to become J.J. Abrams.

George could have stopped at episode six, and if he had, he'd probably still be generally loved rather than generally ridiculed. But life goes on, and a creative fellow like George isn't going to call it quits. So he made Episodes 1, 2, and 3, and had his reputation change from "that cool guy who invented Star Wars" (which he DID do by the way) to "that idiot who ruined Star Wars." And then he got replaced by J.J. Abrams, who made a movie that is cautiously predictable and unoriginal.

And honestly, I missed George. I missed all the random, unnecessary aliens, like that rat who laughed at everything in Jabba's Palace or the Sand People who shot at people during the pod races. I miss his obsession with symbolism and his epic shots of single Jedi going against some monstrous beast or a single rebel facing up against a giant imperial walker. George's world had it's problems, but at least it was a coherent and interesting, not just a random collection of old, recycled favorites thrown together in the most marketable bundle possible. To me, this didn't even feel like a Star Wars movie. I felt like I was watching something from a studio "far, far, away." But this is what we get. We got rid of George Lucas, and now we have a fatherless franchise- a Star Wars world without cohesion or plot, but with a lot of fun explosions and comic relief. And many people are pretty happy about it. But I, for one, am disappointed.

title: A void has opened up in the Force...
review:
As I watched Episode VII, I kept finding reasons to hope. Rey and of course Han Solo and Chewie were well-acted, the yellow golem seemed like a nice character (although she lacks a back story), and on a technical level, it was clear that the execution was more even than in the prequels.

As soon as the opening text began to scroll, though, the worry crossed my mind that I was now in an alternate universe in which Luke and Han and the Sith Lords had watched parts of Episodes IV-VI on video but did not actually live through any of the events in question or learn from them. It was not even clear whether these events had happened at all – apparently the Empire was not defeated, it had merely rebranded itself as the First Order while continuing to terrorize planets with Star Destroyers and stormtroopers. The last two Death Stars had easy-to-find fatal weaknesses and were destroyed, costing the Empire massive losses – Palpatine's heirs therefore decided to build an equally vulnerable but much more expensive Death Star. Meanwhile the not-victorious Rebellion changed its name to the Resistance; it also sent some of its people to create an impotent restored Republic.

At this point, you might think that the movie was concocted in the following way. Ask random people what they remember disliking about Episodes I-III (midichlorians, annoying romance, overly acrobatic lightsaber duels). Ask random people what they remember liking about Star Wars (bar scene with aliens, the Millennium Falcon, Han Solo being a smuggler, cute droids, clambering around in the interior of the Death Star, etc. etc. etc.). Avoid the first and insert the second.

If you were to think that, though, you would be overlooking the genuinely creative ideas that went into this movie. Rather than making the new Sith Lord scary, J.J. Abrams modeled Kylo Ren off of Red Mist from Kick Ass, brilliantly adding curly black hair and a Bane obsession. He reports to a bipedal snail who, presumably worried that people will laugh at him, only appears via hologram, at ten times his normal size.

There is also the family drama: Han and Leia gave birth to an ornery son. Due to this shocking turn of events, Han and Luke (the boy's ex-teacher) are now traumatized and have spent years wasting time while the forces of evil ravage the galaxy.

Another novelty, which has impressed critics ("the movie is self-aware!"), is that characters sometimes make fun of the Star Wars idea. For instance, when the time comes to blow up Death Star 3.0, Han Solo is like, "yeah, yeah, we know how this works, we find the fatal flaw and then blow it up." I'm not sure I understand, though – a big chunk of the movie is consumed regurgitating the Death Star sequence, there is no suspense since we know what will happen, and so are we supposed to be like, "Oh, but J.J. Abrams knows this is unoriginal, so it's actually hilarious and clever"?

Meanwhile, efforts to find deep human emotions, or the sense of something genuinely alien, founder in the void permeating this film. We will maybe have better luck if we try to find in it clues about our own society.

When Kylo Ren discovers that a woman is somehow involved in the story line, he immediately freaks out ("A girl?!"). This reaction is paralleled by a boatload of top-level critics, e.g. Manohla Dargis (NYT): "the images of Mr. Boyega and Ms. Ridley each holding a lightsaber are among the most utopian moments in a Hollywood movie this year." Rey is, however, a more ambiguous character than these writers seem to have noticed.

She is mysteriously amazing at everything, especially fighting, flying unknown spaceships, and using the Force. Since women in real life actually have to work at things, seeing another woman being effortlessly awesome is helpful... how, exactly? On the other hand, when Rey starts having Force visions, she freaks out and runs distraught into the forest. As we know, when confronted with serious emotional challenges, women go to pieces because biology. It is true that Rey is stronger than the other young main characters, Finn and Ren; but since (given their understanding of femininity) the writers made her periodically fragile, that meant making the male roles pathetic. None of this implies criticism of Daisy Ridley, who does what can be done to salvage her character.

Speaking of critics, another way TFA has been of service is in enabling us to understand how people in the Soviet Union must have felt while reading Pravda:

 Mark Kermode (the Guardian): "Consider me conquered... a breathtaking sequel... with genuine heart and soul"

 Peter Travers (Rolling Stone): "... the movie event of the year is here"

 Matt Zoller Seitz (rogerebert.com) "Episode VII... is the film that J.J. Abrams was put on earth to make"

There have, however, been some great analyses submitted by readers on IMDb.

Han Solo's role in this movie can be seen as a metaphor for George Lucas. A powerful figure but with the tragic flaw of being reluctant to listen to other people – if only he had a friend to give him honest criticism while writing Episodes I-III! Finally, after many years, worn out by rejection, he humbles himself enough to surrender his life work to others, people he has reason to distrust but wants to believe in. He is promptly stabbed through the heart by the red sword of Disney.

The movies directed by Lucas did have flaws. There is still more heart in the single scene in Episode II in which a young Boba Fett, alone on the deserted battlefield, cradles his father's severed head, than in this entire movie.

title: I do not possibly think they could have done it worse
review:
I've been on a roll with movies. I've enjoyed the last 5+ movies that I've seen in theaters. In addition, I am a huge Star Wars fan who is even a fan of the prequels.

I went into SW7 thinking there would be no chance I would be disappointed... But I was so amazed by how bad this movie was.

title: Was very excited to see movie, but left very disappointed
review:
Spoilers! I don't have to tell anyone how similar this movie was to A New Hope. At first I didn't mind the similarities one bit. I found them amusing and fun. BB-8 the new R2-D2, Rey with the obvious similarities to Luke Skywalker. When they reintroduced the old Millennium Falcon, I was very much into this movie. But the blatant and deliberate parallels never stop. Every other scene my reaction would be: This is just like... or she reminds me of... all movie long.

There are probably a lot of people who are just fine with the obvious parallels, these same people probably enjoyed the movie very much. Good for you, but I couldn't help but be disappointed. By the time they introduced the 3rd Death Star (yes I know they call it something else in the movie, but its essentially the same thing), the movie had completely lost my interest. Rey's character was about the only thing that felt "new" or interesting.

I do want to point out that the parallels aren't the only reason that I disliked the movie. I though the action was lacking. In modern movies with crazy special effects the plot often isn't given as much emphasis. This can be forgiven if the action is at least top notch. This movie didn't really deliver. I also though that Hans Solo's death was horribly lame. I didn't feel sad or emotionally impacted at all. Is it because I am stone cold at heart. No. I'm the guy who honestly started to tear up at the end of the LEGO movie! The finding Luke underlying plot never seemed all that interesting to me either, though depending on how that plot point develops in future movies I might change my mind. Even ignoring that fact that the movie was basically a retelling of A New Hope I'd say it was an average movie at best.

Whenever you go into a movie with high expectations, you often leave at least a little disappointed, but I never expected to be this totally and completely underwhelmed.

title: Huge disappointment
review:
***IT CONTAINS SPOILERS*** I had high expectations of this new Star Wars movie and I got very disappointed. This movie is a huge fiasco. It brings absolutely nothing new, it lacks imagination, the plot is idiotic, the dialogues are idiotic, the story is a copy cat of Episode IV and an extremely poor one at that: secret information hidden in a droid on a desert planet, the resistance badly needs it and so does the First Order (poorly resembling the Empire); the resistance wants to destroy a new Death Star, just that this one is bigger. And so on.

There is no character development. The new protagonists are so empty of any meaning that you can't relate to them in any way. Very poor acting skills by the new main leads Daisy Ridley (Rey), John Boyega (Finn), Oscar Isaac (Poe Dameron) and Adam Driver (Kylo Ren). The reunion of Han Solo and Leia is so dry and cold as if indeed they are two people with nothing in common than a poor movie script.

They kill off Han Solo BEFORE they build any tension that would make any impact on the audience other than frustration that Harrison Ford leaves the movie. We don't know anything about the conflict between father and son, we don't get to experience the father's struggle to bring his son back, there is absolutely nothing to cause a genuine sense of loss and pain when Han Solo is killed.

The Republic planets are destroyed by the new Death Star and again we feel nothing for it since we did not get any change at all to develop any feeling for the Republic. We only know there is a Republic. So we don't care they get killed.

Why do we have the resistance ?! We already have the Republic. Also the First Order is not a dominating power like the Empire so that you would need a resistance to fight it.

Why is there a hidden map that takes you to Luke Skywalker ? If Luke wanted to disappear, why did he leave a map behind ? or who spied on him and found his location and then produced a hidden treasure map to point his location ? It doesn't make sense. It's just a very poorly written story.

Then PHLEASE !! why do we need the desert planet Jakku that looks identical to Tatooine, sand people and all ? It must be because the writers of the script lack imagination and they copied Episode IV.

The first entrance of the villain Kylo Ren is so ridiculous, he is like a teenager in a Halloween suit. I thought it was a joke. There is no comparison to Darth Vader possible. Darth Vader's entrance was so naturally imposing; Kylo Ren is pathetic. Darth Vader's generals were trembling in fear of him; Kylo Ren gets bullied by his, especially Hux antagonizes him openly and trashes him right in front of the Supreme Leader. Another general disobeys his orders to continue the fight and runs in fear from the bridge. Kylo Ren is indeed puny. In his childish fits of anger all he manages to achieve is vandalize some electronics around the battleship.

Han Solo and Chewbacca appear out of nowhere. At least the writers should have created some reasonable explanation as to why Han Solo and Chewbacca managed to find themselves on the Millennium Falcon immediately as it clears off the planet atmosphere.

And how comes a person who is not a force sensitive - Finn - uses a light-saber AND fights a supposedly well trained Sith lord - Kylo Ren - whom we've seen in the earlier scenes using the Force ! And how comes Rey, who is not trained in the Force, fights and defeats the Sith ? It doesn't matter that "the Force runs strong in her family", she is just not trained to fight. Her fighting skills and use of the Force just come for free out of nowhere.

And what is that rathtar monster doing on Han Solo's ship !? It seems that it's only purpose is to eat the bad guys 'cause the writer needs to get rid of them, otherwise to Finn the rathtar only offers a joy-ride around the ship. Can't eat the main character.

And of the wonderfully diverse Star Wars galaxy all we get to see is a bit of sand, a bit of forest and a bit of sea and they all look so much Earth like.

It seems that J.J.Abrams mocks the Star Wars fans. This movie is so wrong in so many ways, it's a shame it made so much money in the box office. I am rating it 1 because I can't give it 0.

title: very very ordinary
review:
SPOILERS AHEAD

I am truly baffled. This is patently not a good film; but it doesn't suck either. What it is, is a very very ordinary film. I'm torn between 4 or 5 out of ten. It does, however, take a giant d**p all over the lore of the Star Wars universe.

The Good

It looks and sounds nice; I think it does feel like a Star Wars film in this minimal sense. Considering the thinnest of the gruel, some of the acting is quite good (Ford, the two young protagonists). I didn't mind the fan service and some of the comic touches (although some did injure the drama).

The Bad

The 'plot' – are you kidding me? I refuse to believe that anyone could feel anything other than shame for this tedious cut and paste job. I think your average fan-fic writer could do significantly better than this. Actually, I think a couple o' dozen chimps could do better.

'That's not how the Force works'. Quite so. Moments after confirming the existence of the Force, Rey is performing Jedi mind tricks and murderlising Sith Lords (without years of tortuous training, or indeed any training whatever). It doesn't add up. They may explain it in later films, but a character this powerful is a total cop-out. A decent female lead was long overdue, but it should have been developed – AT ALL.

Why exactly did our new Sith Lord turn into an emohawk and a complete p@@@y? I thought he was doing a reasonable job beforehand. I won't criticise the actor, he made the best of a very bad hand.

Almost zero character development. The pace of the film is so quick that we don't get to know any of the characters. We get 15ish minutes of development for the two new protagonists and the main antagonist, and a sprinkling for the rest. A lot of the scenes felt really awkward and unnatural; the worst was Fin reuniting with the pilot guy.

I wonder if Han's walk down that bridge will be his last. We suspected that he was going die during the film, but this was just feeble. I rolled my eyes in the cinema; I wanted to boo (boo!). But the worst bit was that it didn't have any emotional impact. One of the most iconic heroes in film history dies and it barely seemed to have even happened.

The Indifferent

Oh the mysteries (i.e. unanswered questions). I don't actually mind this that much, but I think they probably did go a bit over the top. The dialogue isn't great, but it isn't total garbage. My conclusion: I won't be going to the cinema for the next one; I doubt Disney careI don't have kids to buy tat for. Come back George, all is forgiven. May the force be with you – always!

title: A great example of a defensive movie product
review:
This movie is neither as good as some would like to make you believe nor as bad as some would like to believe themselves.

Basically, it is a product, not a work of art. I'm not in the entertainment industry, so I'm not gonna comment on it's product attributes, I'm not qualified. But, by definition, art is for everybody, so I can comment on it as a work of art, even if it is not such a thing.

There are roughly two parts of the movie:

1. First, where we meet the new characters and learn the new plot, which is a rehash of the old plot(s)

2. Second, where we encounter the old characters and the rehash becomes more of a do-over

First part is fun. Flawed in so many ways, but fun with a few good jokes. Even the plot rehash isn't too bad, as you can justify it as a case of history repeating itself.

Second part is not fun. It is not funny (except for a Chewbacca joke, which is actually in the transition between the first and second part). It so flawed as to become silly. The rehash fails to stand to scrutiny any more and feels too heavy, forced and pointless. Even what was supposed to be a good self-reference joke about putting someone in the garbage disposal with compacting walls, just falls flat, as does the most tragic event soon after that.

I won't go into details, many others already did. It is not just to avoid repeating their insights, but because the movie is designed (it's a product, remember, it is designed) defensively. For anything you try to "attack", there is a way to defend it. But, looking at it as a whole, there's not much worth defending.

It reminds me of Windows 95, which was a rehash of Windows 3.1. What the market wanted and well advertised. It made a lot of money. Like this product will. Of course, as it was really not good, it was soon phased out. Like this product will be, I think.

title: ...and may the force rest in peace
review:
I have never before written a movie review, but after watching this abomination I felt compelled to spread the truth: THE EMPEROR HAS NO CLOTHES!

Now I understand why Disney bought Lucasfilm and with it the rights to Star Wars - they hated its success so much, so that they wanted to destroy it once and for all, but making a lot of money on the way. To be truly efficient they needed to get the sith lord of movie-making J.J. Abrams on their side, whose storytelling talent is that of a log in a fireplace. For hours after watching this so-called movie, I wondered how the story writing was actually done - did they first start with the plot or with the plot holes. The plot holes in SWTFA are so brilliantly executed, so that hundreds of books and Disney cartoons (generating more profits along the way) will be needed to fill in the gaps. While I agree that the plot holes made some sense (in terms of future PROFITS), I cannot say the same about the plot itself - its complete lack of logic is staggering. The next step in their plan of ruining SW was even better - they had to create 2-dimensional uninteresting characters (no need to mention specific ones since they all fit this definition perfectly) that had to be acted very poorly (which explains the subconscious desire of Han Solo to die and relieve Harrison Ford from carrying on with the role). For the picture to be complete they had to add cheesy humor and cheap CGI effects - obviously supreme leader Snoke was so powerful, so that he succeeded to escape the LOTR universe and jump right into the SW one. I don't know why John Williams decided to participate in this plan and ruin his own music, but this time he delivered a completely unmemorable score.

Although my review seems overly critical this move has one redeeming value, that makes up for all its flaws - now, I consider the prequels (SW 1-3) to be true masterpieces of movie-making.

title: Safety in nostalgia (Minor spoiler alert)
review:
Great sci-fi movies are things of wonder. Think Blade Runner, the original Terminator or indeed Episode III - A New Hope. Alas the Force Awakens falls well short of any of these classic theatre fillers.

With modern production comes stunning visuals, it should be expected. This element of the film cannot be faulted with a superb blend of new and old techniques. The cartoon feel of the last three movies is gone, you are fully immersed in the Star Wars universe.

*Minor spoiler alert* So far so good, all we need now is a plot and a dose of great story telling. Shouldn't be a problem with the emotional investment we all have in these characters should it? Well there you would be entirely wrong. Hans Solo, Princess Leia and Chewbacca almost look placed in to the scenes with a desire only to bring authenticity rather than development. Our new 'heroes' are frankly a bit wooden. The idea of Finn and his place in the story is a sound one but Rey lacks any depth for you to really care about what happens to her. As for our main villain Kylo Ren, well I was only really terrified when he took off his mask to reveal 'that' hair do.

So what we're left with is a massive dose of nostalgia, delivered with visual dexterity but falling flat on characters. There is little in fresh ideas on display. A robot ball can hardly be classified as new or interesting. This is Star Wars greatest hits if you will. I enjoyed it for what it was but it's too reverential to it's past and has clearly been created to lay the path for future episodes. Let's hope they will have those shackles removed.

As I write this the movie is rated 8.4 on IMDb meaning it ranks alongside The Shining. Oh dear, that's mass hysteria for you.

title: Was this supposed to be a SEQUEL....or REBOOT? Failed miserably at both....
review:
A small droid carrying classified data crash lands on desert planet. Meets teenage characters. Rebel Alliance needs the data to fight the Empire's new planet-destroying weapon. Rinse and repeat.

Sound familiar? That was the plot to both Episode IV: A New Hope, and Jar-Jar Abrams latest calamity that just found its way onto cinema screens across the country.

I REALLY REALLY REALLY wanted to like this movie-- but alas, we got yet another one of Abrams' typical mind-numbing explosion-fests. It has ALL of Jar-Jar Abrams normal movie failings:

* A cast of characters almost entirely made up of pre-adolescents trying to play adult roles.

* Dialogue/screenplay that seems like it was written by an 8-year old.

* Nothing that even slightly resembles a plot. I am surprised Abrams didn't put "Red Matter" in this movie to fill in all the gaps between his weak story-telling and the plot loopholes it creates, like he did with Star Disaster XI.

As is the case with most of the reboots he has done to date-- Abrams lacks the creativity and writing ability to come up with an original and compelling plot on his own, so he just plagiarizes an existing story and makes "some changes" to better fit his "vision" (as in LSD-induced) of it. He props up these mindless stories by inserting a bunch of unnecessary homage moments to famous lines and clichÃ©s from the previous established films in the mythos to try and give his creation validity ("He's dead, Jim").

Really? Another movie about destroying a death star? A droid carrying the plans that the Empire wants to stop from falling into Alliance hands? How original....

He doesn't care if his stories makes sense or not, or if he breaks his own rules; in Star Trek XI, like when the Enterprise could not beam up Spock's mother (because she was falling), but later in the movie, Scotty and Kirk beamed onto the Enterprise from another solar system while it was moving at warp speed with no problems! The Force Awakens had PLENTY of these "Abrams' moments".

A wise man once told me-- "The litmus test for good and bad storytelling comes down to this: do the actions of the characters in your story fit the background and motivations you gave them in your story history? If not-- it is GARBAGE." For instance, a Romulan captain, so enraged his home planet got destroyed-- would not sit on his hands for 25 years, waiting for Spock (who, given the complexity of time travel-- might NEVER have appeared) to show up, so he can blow up the entire galaxy (obviously Abrams does not understand interstellar distances) just to show everyone just how mad he really is!! Now there is a story that will be remembered over the ages....

The actors in this movie were so poor-- it was difficult to tell what exactly their motivations, passions, and driving ideals were. They all had about as much emotional content as Hayden Christiansen (little or none) from the prequels.

* Explosions and guns ablazing, pretty much from the moment the beginning credits close until the end credits start rolling. By the time you are 5 minutes into the movie-- you are already bored and desensitized to it.

I am not surprised to find that many of the people who thought Star Trek XI and XII (the one with a Caucasian Khanoonian Singh) were good movies, also think this movie was in any way memorable (other than the humongous sense of disappointment I walked out of the theater feeling).

Jar-Jar Abrams should be banned from ruining any more legendary movie franchises. The fans themselves could have written a better story and backdrop for this film.

title: The end of my love for the Star Wars franchise.
review:
***SPOILERS BELOW***

I can't believe I'm saying this, but this movie makes me miss George Lucas. I think we all owe George a huge apology. I didn't care much for the prequels at all, but at least they were original and you can tell there is a passion behind the story and the film-making. You can clearly tell episode 7 was made by the Disney corporate 'machine' and is aimed at leaching money from our nostalgic wallets.

The fans got exactly what they asked for. That is, if they were looking for a movie with Stormtroopers, check. A death star with a vulnerability that can be easily exposed, check. Explosions, check. Numerous chase scenes, check. A story that works around all the above requirements and does nothing to explain what is going on or what our beloved characters have been doing the last 30 years, check.

About an hour in, I felt it was obvious that the movie was rushed and story be damned. Another death star assault? Another cantina scene? (neither which come close to the originals and were totally rushed through) Rey basically becomes a Jedi over the course of 5-10 mins? Poe and Finn become best pals and create a strong brotherly bond after knowing each other for what, 7 mins? I was shocked at how rushed this movie was to accomplish some of its plot goals.

Oh, and there is just as much, or more CGI in this film than the prequels, don't be fooled. Truth is, practical effects take much more time and effort than CGI, and again, this movie feels very rushed, so this should be no surprise. Shooting this movie on film was also a waste of time as it might as well been digital. I mean seriously, for all of the talk about being careful and using CGI sparingly, we somehow get a scene involving 4 terribly over CGI'd tentacle equipped aliens that chase our heroes about 30 â€“ 40 mins into the movie. I think it was one of the worst scenes in any Star Wars movie, period. There are also a few CGI characters (Snoke, the Junk Dealer, Maz) that were totally unnecessary to be CGI, but they did it anyway.

***BIGGEST SPOILER OF ALL TIME BELOW***

How Han Solo was handled was so disappointing. And whatever was done in this regard was going to draw a strong reaction from the fans. And sure, I know Harrison Ford doesn't want to be in the whole trilogy and you all know that he will come to an end in this movie. But the manner in which he meets his end is so tragic in how bad it is. The greatest and most beloved hero of the Star Wars universe dies without a fight, but with a whimper and is then just discarded like a piece of trash. It was an insult to his character. We waited 30 years for THAT? Why bother? It just seemed like a real FU to fans of the original trilogy as in 'You like your Han Solo do you, he's your favourite character and the only redeemable part in this mess of a movie, right? Well, we're going kill him in the most cowardly, pathetic, ill-conceived way we can. The Mouse is in charge now, screw your original trilogy!"

I just don't know why they bothered to have the original heroes in this movie at allÂ…oh wait, I know why, to get a bunch of nostalgic Star Wars fans to shell out their hard earned space bucks in order for Disney to recoup its $4 billion investment asap! Business is business and this movie screams it and reminds you constantly every time the plot is advanced and important details are glossed over.

It saddens me to be so negative about this as I love Star Wars and really like JJ Abrams and I also think Lawrence Kasdan is a genius. All I can think is that Disney had way too much say in the end product in order to satisfy their long term plan of releasing a new film every year, and new toys, books, games, etc. They will ensure this franchise will speak to the lowest common denominator and ensure Star Wars becomes just 'another franchise' in their stable of acquired (and extremely lucrative) franchises.

title: Disney Cash Grab That Offers Very Little To The Star Wars Saga
review:
I went in watching The Force Awakens with extremely high hopes. For one I loved all 6 previous Star Wars movies and this film had all the ingredients for another good one. Kasdan writing the script, the John Williams score, a 200 million dollar budget back by Disney with the latest special effects, and the original cast we all love. My main 12 points of dislike for this movie are:

1. Han Solo's death was predictable and although I had no problem with him dying it was very anti climatic. It was a terrible way for one of the most beloved characters to go out. He didn't die heroically he just simply walked out into the catwalk and died almost as a suicide. At least Harrison finally got his wish.

2. The planets and settings in this movie felt too earth like and boring compared to the prequels and original trilogy. There wasn't anything new we haven't seen before. This also goes for the spacecrafts and the aliens

3. Added no new ideas about the Star Wars universe, the force, or any back story despite taken place 30 years after ROTJ.

4. A very average musical score by John Williams. Maybe one of the bigger surprises of this movie

5. Way too fast pacing. I love non stop action as much as the next guy but it seemed like there was no time to let anything sink in because there was an action scene every 5 minutes with virtually no set up or context.

6. Total lack of respect for the concept behind the force and Jedi training. In movies like Phantom Menace and Empire Strikes Back we see the great importance of the training in the art but now a scavenger with the force learned Jedi tricks on the fly in a matter of a few minutes.

7. Rehashed script from the original trilogy with poor dialogue and pathetic attempts at humor. Not only was there no memorable lines in this film the 3rd Death Star is simply a insult at this point.

8. Weak villains. Kylo Ren was simply a Vader wannabe with a childish temper. Captain Phasma is a shiny female chrome storm trooper that does absolutely nothing in this movie accept tell Finn to put his helmet back on and deactivate a shield without putting up any sort of a fight.

9. Uninteresting CGI characters. Maz, Snoke, and the junk yard dealer. For a film that was empathizing practical effects we get a few CGI characters that don't look any better or worse than the CGI Lucas used over 15 years ago. In fact I found the CGI characters in the prequels far more interesting and better designed.

10. Rey as a super woman Mary Sue. Having a hero that can do anything and who is just as strong or stronger than the main antagonist is just poor writing.

11. Weak light saber battles. The light saber fight in the forest might of looked cool from a cinematic perspective but it was bland and almost hard to take seriously since it was a trained sith fighting a 90 lbs scavenger who was never in a battle before.

12. Too many plot holes, unanswered questions and lack of character motivations. I'm sure we will get a little more explanation in the next movies but it would be nice to know at the beginning why Kylo turned on his parents to try to continue the legacy of his grandfather who he never met. Didn't Han or Lea tell their son that Vader became good again in the end anyways? Or also why Finn suddenly had a change of heart after growing up a brainwashed stormtrooper?

title: More Plot Holes than holes in a Cheese Factory in Switzerland!!!

Been a big fan of the originals I left the cinema disappointed, here's why.

Don't get me wrong there were some things about this film that were good but unfortunately there were a lot more things, the more important things, that I thought were terrible and ruined it for me.

Visually there is no question that it was a stunning film, however, the story and characters lacked all depth, something that every other star wars film had. The story for me was scatty, it didn't flow it just skipped from one thing to another with no real explanations or background information, things just seem to randomly happen like R2D2 suddenly waking up at the end and pulling part of a star map from his rear end, why, how? or Han Solo who could have literally been anywhere in the galaxy randomly capturing the millennium falcon as it just entered space.

The main bad guy Kylo Ren started off great but then later I just felt like he was a 14 year kid playing dress up. Darth Vader wore a mask to keep him alive because he was brunt, battered, arm and legless, there was no reason why Kylo Ren was wearing a mask apart from to dress up like Darth. In my opinion he should have never taken the mask off and if he did there should have been a scarred and battered ruined face underneath that gave him a real reason to wear it other than just to dress up like Darth.

There was way too much concentration on special effects and action and no where near enough story depth, explanation, information and character background. Too much time running around from random monsters, flying about in constant battles, way overly dramatic acting and unnecessarily long lingering camera shots and pointless, lazy, unnecessary filler scenes. Too big a budget, all spent on effects with an un-engaging very weak story.

This would have been much better as two films with much more story explanation, information and character development, a slower paced and more gradual build-up to the end rather than just all out cram as much CGI action in as you can style movie.

The fact that this movie has managed to score an 8.8 at the time of writing this review on IMDb also highlights to me the sheer level of corruption, dishonesty and general misleading false reviews paid for and written by the main stakeholders of this movie. I refuse to believe that the average intelligence of the human race has fallen so low that out of all the genuine reviews of this movie it's genuinely scored an 8.8.

I have no doubt that a portion of the budget for this film has been spent on writing disingenuous reviews and fixing ratings to increase the hype and generate more revenue, it's a sad state of affairs. You only have to read some of the reviews for yourself to see it, it's very blatantly obvious. This is the only reason why I've given it a 1 to attempt to balance the un-proportional number of fake 10's otherwise it would probably be a 2 or 3.

Because of a mistake with my ticket bookings I ended up watching this movie for free with premium seats, I almost went and asked for my money back anyway to pay for the 2 1/2 hours of my life I'll never get back. This may sound a bit harsh but it reminded me of Transformers 4 and I had to stop watching that before the end it was so bad.

title: A boring and poorly done mash-up of ideas borrowed from the original trilogy
review: OK, this is my first review on IMDb and I had to do this. Im a big fan of Star Wars (Episode I-VI), I love both the original and the newer trilogies. I have my own ranking of all 6 movies, but I enjoyed them all for one main reason - they were entertaining. The series was full of new and original ideas, interesting characters and scenes that lingered on your mind long after you left the movie hall. Episode VII fails as a movie first - there is no character development, no original plot or ideas, its just a poorly done mash-up of ideas and scenes that made Episodes IV-VI so successful. You will not for once find yourselves thinking 'wow that scene was awesome' or 'that character was so cool' or 'that was an interesting twist'. I watched 'Jurassic World' a few months ago, Yes it was yet another movie about dinosaurs wreaking havoc on a remote island resort - but I loved every minute of it because it was entertaining and engaging. JJ Abrams and Co have been so busy concentrating on getting the VFX, costumes and sets to match the original trilogy accurately in an attempt to please hardcore fans. But in doing that they've distracted themselves from the essential elements that make a movie - 'a movie'. Star Wars VII as a movie is boring and predictable at best.

title: Star Wars, The Force Awakens - Contains spoilers
review:
** Update, I would like to say that I am extremely grateful that I did not spend the money on seeing this movie in a theater. I watched at home on a purchased DVD for about half the cost. And that my friends, is 3 hours of my life that I will NEVER get back. Lawrence Kasden ought to be ashamed of himself for the casting of this movie. Dude, you have done better.

Let me start by saying I am NOT a Star Wars fanatic, role player, costume wearing geek. I am 55 years old and stood in line out in front of a theater in Seattle to watch the original episode 1(IV) like millions of other people and with it being the mid to late 70's, the excitement and the technology was unmatched by anything at the time.

We all thought it was cool, revolutionary, uncharted territory. It was a space western with good vs bad I'll give you that nevertheless, it was still cool.

I agree with a lot of the contributors, that this is more of a reboot than a sequel. This is also, not a movie that could stand on its own.

You can definitely feel and see the absence of George Lucas. He belongs there. This is his property and he is the essence and spirit of Star Wars.

My opinion on the story, concept was OK but not great. Again it was a rehash of Rey doing the Luke thing from a desert planet. Don't get me wrong, I did think the action was exciting, the weapons were cool, and the new ships were great. But I think that's where my enjoyment of the movie ended.

The writers should have their pay chopped up into little pieces. The actors should have questioned the garbage they were told to speak. The casting director should be fired. The producers and directors should be embarrassed. And frankly, those statements are sugar coated.

I think the choice of actors for some roles were way off the mark.

Kylo Ren - Adam Driver had no resemblance or qualities of his parents whatsoever. The actor himself was totally unconvincing as a conflicting being moving ever further to the dark side. He was a let down.

Finn - John Boyega was also not convincing in his role either. He really did not pull off the "former" storm trooper who was confused about his place in the universe, just that he "did the right thing" and that he needed to run. He definitely needs to return to acting school.

Poe Dameron - While Oscar Isaac is adorable, he over acted every scene he was in. As if he was trying way too hard. And finding out, today, that he was the same guy in Ex-Machina?? Wow, uh, there are no words. Ever heard of Stella Adler Academy of acting and Theater? Or any other acting teachers?

Lor San Tekka - Sometime during the next 2 or 3 movies, I hope they explain who and what he was. Otherwise it was a HUGE waste of an incredible talent in Max Von Sydow.

My overall opinion on this episode is this. If the makers were looking for a comic book style, campy movie that was not to be taken too seriously, they succeeded swimmingly. If they were looking for it to have a more serious effect on the movie goers, it was an epic fail.

One really cool standout character that I hope returns for other episodes is Maz Kanata. Lupita, you rocked that role.

Daisy Ridley performed well and embodied Rey.

Some of the old characters such a Admiral Ackbar were also nice to see again. Chewy, C3PO, and BB8 were pretty good.

Carrie Fisher and Harrison Ford phoned it in.

I sure the hope the next movie is better. It's been a long road following the story since 1977. Don't wreck it for those of us that have been there since the beginning.

Let's put it this way. Having been born in 1960, I grew up in a TV watching and movie going household. Saw every Disney movie ever made, and have spent thousands of dollars on others as well. So, as a longtime consumer, I feel that my opinion probably counts.

title: Reasons why I didn't like it
review:
Now I am by no means the biggest Star Wars fan but I enjoyed the original series for what it was and even the prequels because it still felt like Star Wars to me. This, however, did not.

My number 1 biggest complaint: There was no star. The 2 main characters felt very much like secondary characters to me, with no one for them to support. If the original series had only Han Solo and Princess Leia, something would seem missing right? A leader! and that's Luke Skywalker. He carries those movies and Han and Leia are great characters but Luke is the star. This movie has no star.

My number 2 complaint: Too much humor. The original series did not even come close to having this much humor. Some of it was funny, but often they were trying too hard and it was cringe-worthy and when you have that much comedy, you're taking away from the epic fantasy that Star Wars is supposed to be.

The rest of my complaints: CG. Now don't be a hypocrite, because a lot of people say they hated the prequels and their CG but ya know what, this movie had a ton of it too and many many characters were pure CG when they could've easily been done in makeup and it would have been much more effective. Too many fake looking monsters.

No arm dismemberment. What the hell? That is a staple of Star Wars. Someone always gets their arm cut off and I was so waiting for that to happen with Kylo and it never did. I know this is PG-13 but I think you can still do that.

Kylo Ren looked good with his mask, although a little funny without his hood, and even funnier without his mask. Looked like a Harry Potter villain to me. And where did that light saber come from? A little back story please.

The black overtones. Are we really still doing this? This is Star Wars, not Race Wars. Moment's like, "You don't know where I come from and what I've seen. They'll destroy us all." Being called a "Traitor" that made it seem like he was being called the N word. Being 'whipped' by Kylo Ren in the back with his light saber. I'm sure a lot of people won't agree with this but to me it seemed all too apparent. I want to watch a movie that puts me in a fantasy world and not being constantly reminded about the black vs. white in this country.

Besides the returning cast members, everyone in this movie is under 40. The originals had mature legends like Peter Cushing and Alec Guinness. I'm so tired of Hollywood not paying respect to veteran actors. Max Von Sydow appears in the first 5 minutes but he is killed off and underused like so many other characters. No back story given to any of them.

To me this movie suffers all too much from what plagues most other modern movies. It's just a bunch of stuff that happens but nothing is enticing or pulling me in to the actual movie. George Lucas had a vision, and a great sense of artistry. I didn't get that at all here. Seemed to me like a big budget fan film with a lesser quality in every way possible.

title: Another failed attempt to recapture the magic
review:
In 1999 Star Wars creator George Lucas finally began to give us his view on the events that led to Star Wars IV, V and VI. The first Star Wars trilogy was, as we all know, a milestone in cinema history and it's not easy to top something like that. He didn't succeed to top the original trilogy and although successful commercially, fans weren't all to impressed with the prequels. The story was flat, the characters annoying and the special effects too clean. It could be that this even led to his decision to sell off his Lucasfilm and all the rights to the Star Wars imperium. Disney picked up those rights. Maybe because they thought they could do better. Well, commercially they were right. But better films? Their first installment isn't that impressive. It's worse than The Phantom Menace.

Let's get one thing straight: even though it picks up 30 years after Star Wars VI, this is not a sequel. This is a remake. J.J. Abrams tries to get back to the feel of the original trilogy. But essentially copies the storyline of Star Wars IV A New Hope. Okay, so that's disappointing. But let's see where this goes. Abrams then proceeds to give us some awkward comic relief scenes, deep friendships within two minutes of meeting each other and some wooden dialogue. The new bad guy is a spoiled brat who has a tendency for tantrums (and commands the largest army in the galaxy?) and a Supreme Leader who is a hologram. Too make a long story short: I wasn't all too impressed. It's just another failed attempt to recapture the magic of the much loved first three films from the seventies and eighties.

Was it all bad? No, off course not. Abrams knows how to direct action and impress with fine special effects. The casting of John Boyega is a courageous move and commercially smart. Too bad that his character comes off as more annoying than brave. Same goes for the character Kylo Ren. That I am not a fan off Adam Driver does not help either. Newcomer Ridley does hit the right tone and impresses as the new lead character. The familiar faces of Han Solo, Princess Leia and Chewbakka appear, but does that help? They don't bring anything new or fresh. Except for one pivotal scene near the end, which to be fair, was very well done.

It's the first installment, maybe it needs to gain momentum. But The Fellowship of the Ring and Star Wars IV were first installments too and they impressed the hell out of people. There are two other films coming in the next years. But this first one just is not all it's hyped up to be.

title: A soulless film and beyond lazy writing
review:
**To restate, after the first paragraph this review contains spoilers.**

I've never before written a review on IMDb, but considering the very, very undeserved 8.8 rating this movie currently has, and the fact that Disney should basically be sued for false advertising makes me feel compelled to do so.

To begin, as stated abundantly by everyone else posting here, this movie is a remake/rehash/ripoff of Episode IV, A New Hope, masquerading as a sequel. Mentioning the parallels isn't necessary, as they are too numerous and impossible to miss anyway.

What makes this movie really bad are the many plot holes and inconsistencies, I always thought it was a cardinal sin in the movie industry to not obey the laws of your own universe, but for J.J. Abrams and Disney this rule seems not to apply. It does make suspension of disbelief impossible and the whole ride quickly becomes too cringe-worthy to watch, let alone enjoy.

Also the pacing and beat of the film is off and all over the place, making it hard to follow what is really going on. Add to this very limited and confused exposition given as to the current political/power landscape - and it all makes for strained and restless viewing.

Another major issue is that J.J. Abrams doesn't seem to know or care for proportionality or even the flimsiest thread of realism. J.J. Abrams' Star Wars universe seems more like a small village where everyone finds each other in minutes (often through absurd coincidence rather than through intent or crafted story), habitable planets are conveniently lined up within a few hundred thousand miles of each other and the gratuitous mass genocide of I imagine billions (by what to me looked like a pair of buttocks in space, et tu, Disney?) is met with a mild gasp.

The character arcs and motivations are also slip-shot and flimsy. The protagonist seems to be good at everything she tries with no effort or training whereas the antagonist gets progressively weaker throughout the film to the point of just seeming feeble. In fact everything about the new Empire e.g. the First Order, was just downright cartoon-like. In Episode IV, Grand Moff Tarkin's justifications, though of course obscene, were chillingly delivered and convincing. In episode VII however we're treated to a scene reminiscent of a cartoon version of 'Triumpf des Willens' with a horribly over-acting Domhnall Gleeson as General Hux. It made the whole First Order seem to be run by hysterics ordering around an army of myopic stormtroopers. A believable and intimidating opponent it makes not.

So what was good about the movie? Though cute, BB-8 seemed too much like Wall-E had been thrown into the movie and was specifically designed for toy sales, so no points there. Some of the jokes were good, but so poorly timed and constant that not only did they loose their own impact, they ruined the impact of many scenes that were meant to scare or get you invested in the characters. Leaving just some of the sets. The shots of Jakku with the downed Star Destroyers were impressive, but at the same time that summarizes this film for me; watching the downed wreck of a once great saga in a lifeless, soulless film, deserted of any magic or artistry.

I'd give it a -10, as Disney obviously treated this production, and the hopeful viewer, as nothing more than a cash cow without so much as trying to offer anything new or of substance in return. A criminal production.

ps. Regarding acting, the one shot of Darth Vader's molten and charred mask had the most stage presence of all. 'nuff said.

review:
Aside from the Classic Star Wars aesthetic that was very well incorporated in this new installment, there is really not much else to look forward to.

Most scenes felt like a repetition of the previous, with an exception to changes in atmosphere. Other than that, the same three- part pattern was there: Characters verbally narrate the "Why's" and "How's" of the story, nostalgic references or characters are thrown in to help the audience feel as if the story is more intricate or clever than it truly is. Finally, the characters find a way to transport themselves to another planet or place, and the pattern repeats itself over again.

In a way, the entire thing felt like an experimental development of the Star Wars Universe. There are numerous settings with a diverse range of characters, but the writing is bland, and most of the acting, except from Rey and Fin is mediocre at most. Numerous wide shots expound on well-thought out atmospheres, but this in no way justifies the lack of narrative depth.
