title: Boring, Predictable, Disappointing
review:
I've never been a huge fan of the series, but I definitely remember enjoying the first three that came out back in the 70's. For what it was, it was amazing. This new one fails on so many levels.

Warning: Spoilers!

1). The Characters: The new characters (Fin and Rey) are not well built, and the story does very little to give us any emotional connection to these guys. Everything is really fast paced, and there was so much focus on the action, that the character development lacked big time. The other new guy, Poe, with all of his 15 minutes of air time, failed to connect as well. They all seemed to be best buds and super close, but with little dialogue and story to support it (like when Lea was hugging Rey at the end... they barely met). The hero characters were very poorly done, and where I don't dislike them, there's no draw to them either.

Then there's the bad guy, Kylo Ren. I was completely disappointed when he finally decided to remove his mask. He's just an Emo Kid... So lame, so very lame. I want more from the villain perspective than some whiny twenty something goth kid.

2). Predictability: The story and action are completely predictable. Although the graphics (especially 3D) were amazing, there was zero suspense due to the complete predictability of the script. I knew Hans Solo was going to die when Kylo Ren walked out onto that bridge with no side bars (poor design on the Death Star 3.0). I found myself bored, and counting down the minutes when I could leave the theatre.

3). Overtones of Disney Feminism: As a disclaimer, I will say I support equal rights and treatment amongst all races and gender. With that said, the last few Disney movies I've watched (Frozen being the other one) have a strong theme of stupid male lead character, and a strong heroic independent woman character. And thats fine to an extent, we can do away with the damsel in distress theme, but I have a hard time buying the whole thing, or at least how it was executed here. In this case, a scrawny female orphan, who has been getting scrap parts from wreckage all these years, can all of a sudden fight off stronger men, shoot with amazing accuracy when she's never really used a gun, pilot and fix the Millennium Falcon without training and better than Hans Solo (yeah right), and be an absolute master of both The Force and the Lightsaber. It was a disgrace to the old films, where Luke spent a long time in training to master The Force. Some how, our new female hero here just gets it, and beats Emo Kylo Ren in a Lightsaber battle... even though Kylo Ren spent time training under Luke Skywalker... just so unbelievable, even in a fantasy setting. Horribly executed. I guess it was more important to portray women just as capable, if not better, than writing a believable script.

So in conclusion, it was fun to watch for the 3D action, but very little else. The only characters I liked were the old ones, and they killed a few of those off. So I will probably wait for the DVD release of the next one, before running to watch the second installment of this now horrible series.

title: Recycled Retreading Relived Remake
review:
I've always been in the minority that liked I-III. Sure there were the gaffs like Jar-Jar, but on the whole they had a fascinating story to tell and didn't retread over old ground. You can quibble about how the tale of the Jedi, the origins of the Empire, the Storm Troopers, and the Emperor were told, but it was interesting to see all of this fleshed out. And the development of Annakin Skywalker was well conceived and far more believable than I suspect many of the critics could make it if they had a pen, paper, and a hundred years to write. And, now that I've seen Episode VII, I can confidently say that the best is behind us.

Clearly inspiration was gone and the only thought put into producing this movie was to how to remix tried and true formulas in a different enough way that it could be sold as a new episode rather than a remake. I won't bother with the gory details of all the parallels, which would only serve to label this review as containing spoilers and to decrease the internal stability in my digestive tract. Element after element was shamelessly copied from Episode IV. Apparently the idea was not to give the generation that grew up with the originals something more, but to give the latest generation a Star Wars of its own, relying on the elements that Lucas's genius put together the first time around to work again.

And, unsurprisingly, they do. Behold the average rating of the movie, nearly as high as the original. And given the harsh critical response all around to Episodes I-III, who can blame them? Clearly ingenious storywriting, beautiful special effects, and bold venturing into new narrative territory were not rewarded in the modern cinema marketplace. What's going to rake in the money is tired repetition of the same formulas, perhaps with a few more explosions per minute added in.

title: Decent Acting, Bad Script
review:
This now tops Episode I as the worst Star Wars movie ever. Yes, it's that bad.

It's not bad enough that they rip off elements of other SW movies (other reviews give details, so I won't repeat them here), they add in a lot of things that just "happen" to be in the right place at the right time, and give people abilities that just don't make sense in the SW universe.

Example: the droid that everyone is depending on to get the stolen plans to the Rebellion (sound familiar?) just HAPPENS to stumble across the path of the one woman on the whole planet who is force sensitive. On, right...there's no coincidences with the Force. In episode 4, there was a good reason for Luke finding the droids - they were trying to get to Obi Wan, who we find out later is watching over Luke. But in this movie there's absolutely no explanation except it just happened that way.

Example 2: a guy who has no previous experience with the Force using a lightsaber to defend against a trained Sith. It should have looked more like the scene between the two friends in "The Count of Monte Cristo" and lasted about 3 seconds, not 3 minutes or so.

Example 3: A woman who has no experience with the force suddenly learning that she can move objects with her mind, or use the force to thwart attempts from a trained Sith to infiltrate her mind.

Example 3 (huge spoiler alert): Same woman who has no training whatsoever is able to kill a Sith Lord.

Also, the Sith Lord acts more like a spoiled rebellious teenager than a true Sith. The whole thing just seems finagled together in such a haphazard way as to just be sad. The story is not original, the plot line is sub-par when it's not being a direct rip-off, and the acting is mediocre. If it didn't have the Star Wars title, this movie wouldn't last in the theaters more than three weeks.

I can only pray that the sequel (episode VIII) is better.

title: After Many Years of Waiting, This is the Star Wars Film you are Looking For...
review:
Star Wars Episode VII: The Force Awakens is directed by former Star Trek director J.J. Abrams and focuses around a scavenger (Daisy Ridley), a runaway stormtrooper (John Boyega) and the former war hero Han Solo (Harrison Ford) as they search for the key to destroying the newly-formed First Order, Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill). Overall, I am a huge Star Wars fan who knows quite a thing or two about the franchise (not to brag). When I first found out about this film being under production, I was very excited, yet nervous as Star Wars films have had their bad days. Now, after two years of reflecting on the film, I think I am finally ready to get my opinion out there.

Pros: When watching this movie for the first time, I noticed that the cinematography in this was very different from the Prequel Trilogy. It gave you this feeling that every second screamed adventure and did not feel so contained and dull like the Prequel Trilogy. For example, this movie contains a lot of quick pan overs that were frequently used during the more exciting scenes. Yet, this movie knows when to stop using those when, for example, there is character development going on, which is another huge plus in this movie. The chemistry between all of these characters is great and, as a viewer, I did not dislike any character in the movie and enjoyed everyone in it. I especially enjoyed the main villain in this movie, Kylo Ren (Adam Driver), whomst I feel is very underrated as a villain in this universe. The character himself is not your tipical Star Wars villain like Darth Vader or Darth Revan, but is torn between doing good or being a servant to Supreme Leader Snoke (Andy Serkis). Otherwise, I enjoyed every single character, whether it be Rey, Finn, Poe Dameron, Max Kanata or Kylo Ren, who is a fresh breath of air for Star Wars antagonists themselves.

Cons: This film, although an enjoyable one, does suffer from a few plot flaws. Many people have been bashing the movie's plot for being a total rehash of the original Star Wars. Although the plot was somewhat of a rehash, it wasn't a bust for me at all, although I felt that it did take it to far at points. The prime example of this is Starkiller Base. This is probably one of the laziest things I have seen in a Star Wars film as it feels like a plot point that doesn't quite fit into the story itself, which focuses around finding Luke Skywalker. In other words, it does not have that feeling of importance that the Death Star had in the original Star Wars as that was a huge focus for that plot. Overall, Starkiller Base is just another lazy attempt at making yet another super weapon and is of little significance to the story. Although people may have found other cons to this movie, I personally did not find anything really worth pointing out in this review that is terrible. I think everything else was well done in this movie, whether it be the CGI or the battles, and it surely did entertain me as a whole.

Final Verdict: Star Wars Episode VII: The Force Awakens definitely brought audiences back to a galaxy far, far away in a safe, yet great way that was very much faithful to the original Star Wars trilogy. I have to say that J.J Abrams did a great job with this movie and, although making some mistakes like Starkiller Base, was solid overall and I do suggest seeing it before Star Wars Episod VIII: The Last Jedi comes out later this year.

title: Attack of the clone

If it was an attempt to please old faithful fans - that's a win. If it was an attempt to make a movie - well, that's an obvious fail.

Episodes 1,2 and 3 have set certain level of special effects, both in terms of quality and quantity. Overall impression is that the galaxy has entered some post apocalyptic stage since the end of old good Republic. Huge relic machinery, tube electronics and spaceship dashboards so lame that they make the one of ford f-150 look like triumph of high-tech.

There're only two light spots in this movie - Han Solo and overall decent acting performance of the rest of the crew.

And very personal thing - I will never forgive creators of the movie for having unique chance of letting all three original characters meet each other on the screen and eventually failing to do that.

title: Apparently the fourth highest-grossing film of all time... Why?
review:
So after many years I finally decided to watch this movie and when it was over I just had to breath. What the ... did I just watch? It's one of those movies that just makes me want to write a review just to share my pain and warn others who haven't watched the movie yet to just keep ignoring it. At the end I made a list of dumb moments because unlike others I'm not someone who forgets what just happened 5 minutes ago, a.k.a. the average fan Disney feeds this schlock to. So to keep this review "short" (turned out not to be so short in the end) I will just point things out that I have noticed in a list:

1. So the Millennium Falcon just happens to be on Jakku. Because "HEY LOOK! IT'S THE MILLENNIUM FALCON!" Rey and Fin escape and like an hour later (in movie time) Han and Chewie just happen to find them like they were "just at the right place in the galaxy at the right time". They later explain this is because "They were easy to track, just imagine what would've happened if the First Order found you first." Then why DIDN'T the First Order find them first with the vast amount of resources at their disposal? No, apparently an elderly man and his aging dog-man find them because "HEY LOOK! IT'S HAN AND CHEWIE!"

2. That frigging Star Killer base. First of all, how was this base so secretly built when it appears to have been right in the neighborhood of the Republic home worlds? Then the whole scene when it destroyed those planets was just slapped into the movie like
  • "Ok, Han, Fin and Rey are now on this planet... what can happen?"
  • "I know, let's use the Star Killer base and let it destroy some stuff so everyone knows that the First Order is BAD, it can even be seen from the secret hideout planet our main cast is on with the naked eye because why not?"
Later it's explained that it needs the sun to charge and fire. Okay, but then how does it fire again when the sun is depleted? Does it have engines to move around in space? Why doesn't the whole ecological system of the planet go nuts when the sun is suddenly gone? And why does it have a shield that can be easily penetrated by any ship capable of faster than light travel... you know, ANY ship in the Star Wars universe? The resistance shows up at the base with what feels like 15 X-Wing's piloted by emotionless buffoons. "HEY LOOK, LIGHTSABERS!"

3. Apparently Rey is great at everything. For being raised as a scavenger on a lone desert planet she can fly ships, use hand guns with impressive accuracy, fight and win with a lightsaber against someone who had years more experience than her, use the force to mind-trick people when she feels like it AND just happened to find Luke's lightsaber in a dusty old box by pure luck after walking into some shady bar and hearing a baby cry. What the ...?

4. When Chewie, Fin and Han get captured by the First Order on the forested hideout planet they get instantly rescued by the resistance. "HEY LOOK, X-WINGS!" Han meets Leia after many years yet both characters lack any emotion. They just hug each other, not even a kiss even though they are supposed to be a couple. All these characters in the movie feel just as lifeless and dead inside as the people who made this film were in reality.

5. Poe meets Fin at the resistance outpost after he was supposedly killed in the crash landing on Jakku at the beginning of the movie. The only explanation given how he survived was literally just "I woke up at night, no ship, you were gone... but BB-8 just told me you completed my mission, good boy!" What in the holy mother of god kind of explanation is that? I still don't know how he got off that planet. Last thing we saw was that the First Order destroyed everything on Jakku, ships, encampments, equipment... did he just hitchhike back to the resistance base and then be at the hideout planet in just the right time to rescue Fin and company? Yeah... no.

6. You want me to believe Captain Phasma, this super hardcore storm trooper captain, just deactivated the shield of the super important Star Killer base thing after Fin and Han told her so while pointing a gun to her head? I expected her to tell them "Go F' yourselves, kill me and you will never disable those shields!" but she just does it. Rey wasn't in the scene so a possible mind trick of Phasma by her is impossible. The scene ends with a forced reference to A New Hope.

7. Han Solo dies and Fin and Rey CRY like they've known him for years and not just a few hours. I guess he was "Rey's father she never had"... Okay? This guy she just met and had a boring adventure or two with is now a father substitute for her all of the sudden? All they did was scream at each other while trying to survive one thing after the other. Guess Han offered Rey a job at one point and she was excited? Nah, I don't buy it, they cry because all the man babies in the cinema were crying and so Rey could have an emotional moment when she was fighting Kylo Ren a moment later. "HEY LOOK, HAN SOLO IS DEAD! LIGHTSABERS!"

8. BB-8 randomly removes a piece of cloth from a deactivated R2D2 in a scene for no reason. C3PO tells him some stuff about Luke but who cares, not even a minute later the scene is already over. At the end of the movie R2D2, for some reason, comes back to life and is then used as a deus ex machina so the resistance can have the entire map to Luke's whereabouts because the creators forgot that they basically destroyed all the other important map parts the First Order had with the Star Killer base. I guess this is why the first scene with R2D2 felt so out of place, like it was added late in production when the makers had no idea how the resistance could now find Luke without the First Order maps.

9. Then at the last minute Rey travels in not even a minute of hyperspace to where Luke is hiding in a desperate attempt to mimic Luke's plot to find Yoda in the original trilogy. She finds him and BOOM, the movie's finally over. What an anticlimactic ending. What a relief. "HEY LOOK, IT'S LUKE!"

Oh boy, this is getting too long for my taste so I'm stopping here. I'm planning on watching the other two movies as well but I definitely won't review them like I did this one or else I would still be typing by tomorrow seeing how this was supposed to be the "best one" of the trilogy. I will just leave my star for them and go on my merry way. When people told me these movies were made for stupid people I couldn't believe them, that they would be that bad but after watching this "thing" myself all I can say is that humanity is heading in the right path for extinction.

title: A Good Movie, Just Not a Good Star Wars Movie
review:
Before I begin my review, I would like to warn readers that there are spoilers.

The action in the movie started rather quickly, and within five minutes I was seeing stormtroopers, laser battles, and lightsabers all over again. For some reason, though, I felt a little let down. Something about it didn't feel like the Star Wars I had grown up with. However, I put my doubts aside and told myself that I just needed to wait. I would soon find myself in the Star Wars universe. Unfortunately it never really happened.

Several problems plague Star Wars VII, but there was one main problem that ruined the experience for me. The Force Awakens played out like a reboot of the franchise. The film was undeniably a copy and paste of the 4th and 6th films all the way down to a droid with vital information. Now some may disagree with me on this, but everyone must admit that there are several similarities between the films. Others would say that they liked how it was like a reboot and I would be okay with it except for a few large issues.

My first issue is that because it functioned as a reboot while keeping individuals from previous movies, it really sacrificed the character of those individuals. I grew up watching movies about a farmer's son growing up to become a man, a scoundrel developing a heart, and a princess falling in love. Luke, Han, and Leia developed amazing character over episode 4, 5, and 6. Yet when we come to 7 they have lost what they gained. It's heartbreaking to see these heroes portrayed this way just so that it flows with the story allowing Han to take the role of Ben Kenobi and Luke to take the role of Yoda.

My second issue revolves around Star Wars lore. In the movie, the character Rey discovers that she has force powers. So far this is complying with Star Wars lore. However, later on Rey performs some complicated force powers with no training. This goes against the very nature of the force. Now I am not saying this because I am a guy and don't like to see female leads who can handle themselves. In Star Wars lore, whether in the movies, books, or other mediums, the force isn't something that you can just use on the spot. It takes years of dedication to in order to master it. The fact that she was able to perform a jedi mind trick is almost absurd. It took Luke an entire movie, hence several years, in order to move his lightsaber when in the Wampa cave during episode 5. To have Rey do it without so much as a struggle is an insult.

Another issue that arose is the inconsistent story. About half way through the movie, it is revealed that Kylo Ren is Han and Leia's son and that he turned against Luke's jedi academy and, with the help of the Knights of Ren, burned it to the ground. Yet later on in the movie, Kylo Ren faces off against Rey, who has no training in the art of combat, and she beats him. I personally was left flabbergasted because of the inconsistency. I know that Kylo was injured, but he is a Sith apprentice. They are trained through the use of pain. That's how they learn to use their anger in combat. Sith will train by punishing weakness and if you die in the process they simply say that you were too weak to become a Sith. The scene could have easily been fixed to make it more believable. When Kylo reaches for Skywalker's lightsaber they should have had the lightsaber pass Kylo and fall into the hands of Luke instead of Rey. It would have involved some serious script rewrites but would have allowed for a much more believable and epic scene. Looking at it from a writer's perspective, this would have made a lot more sense. When depicting a villain who will appear in several films, you don't let him get beat during his first meeting with the protagonist. It lessens the tension of the movie and destroys almost any chance of fear towards that villain.

The last main issue I have with the movie is that Disney played it safe. I know that there was a lot of pressure on the company to create something that would be appease everyone, but George Lucas didn't make Star Wars the hit it is today by playing it safe. George Lucas took a personal vision and made it a reality. He showed us an amazing galaxy far away, introduced new and interesting aliens, and gave us outstanding battles. If he had played it safe, Star Wars would have been seen as a sub-par version of Star Trek and not the amazing experience it is today. I know that Disney wanted to create something that everyone would appreciate, but in doing so they created a film that felt like a sup-par knock-off of the 4th film.

Although I was disappointed with the film with all its flaws, there were a few moments when I saw the Star Wars I know and love. I wasn't entirely sold on the acting, however, Oscar Isaac did a solid job acting and John Boyega's performance, although occasionally carried away by his enthusiasm for Star Wars, was memorable. Despite my dislike for the 7th film, I still believe the next film has a chance at being great. I will watch it when it comes to theaters, but if Rey or Finn lose a hand or the film begins on a snow covered planet I will most likely give up on the series.

title: A homage that didn't quite hit home.
review:
Star Wars: A Force Awakens (Don't. Spoilers.)

JJ Abrams pays a silent homage to the death of cinema. A quiet admittance that the school of the old has finally given way to the barren, empty landscape of the new. Lucas based his masterpiece on ground- breaking works of Kurosawa's The Final Fortress. This 'new' trilogy however, boorishly begins by playing to the dying notes of its last installment. Same story- scape but out-of-tune and out-of-date.

The film slowly turns its pages of rotting parchment with establishing shots of a broken landscape. Desert. Dry. Barren. Fallen AT-AT walkers. A TIE fighter in pieces. A downed Star Destroyer. No doubt representing the futility of getting anything out of this new story. Poking fun at the rise of numerous celebrities with anything but talent, the story unfolded with faceless, expressionless characters. Young. Unknown. Unfamiliar. In the setting sun of the Jakku desert, one can almost imagine Abram's sillouette in the distance, hands pulling out the empty pocket fabric, bemoaning, 'Look. That's all I've got. Take it and leave.' Once in a while, he'll throw the remeniscing audience a bone. 'Look. Here's your wookie. And there, the millennium falcon. You happy now?'

Here goes the conversation with the cousin when the credits rolled:

Cousin: He didn't need to go confront him, did he?

Me: He didn't. I tell you it's the wife's fault.

I tried to conceptualise the story arc after Episode VI, V and IV in 1999. Childish no doubt. Here's how I would do one part of it today.

Story would have opened in the Cantina, the new main character trying to cut a deal on a second hand spaceship. Talks failed and as the new guy, street- wise, (like a certain smuggler we were once familiar with) tries to worm his way out of the deal, when none other than that same smuggler appearing with his hairy apprentice and pulls him out of the Mexican stand-off. 'It is MY SHIP!' He bellowed. And the newly formed three stooges blast their way through bounty hunters. There you have it. The Solo Entrĕ.

Sure beats suddenly dropping him on the falcon. Alas.. I'm no Abrams. And I'm pretty sure I'm sounding too full of myself here. But I really expected a little more. Just because it worked, it doesn't necessary make it as good by compressing all three parts back into one.(It cannot be a coincidence that this installment consists of the environments present in the original one. Audiences experienced the deserts of Tatooine, the frost of Hoth and the forestry of Endor) It is a fancy idea, I'm not gonna argue with that. But every other attempt to impress feels like one failed CPR after another. When the Empire Struck Back or when the Jedi Returned amongst others, they all followed the same simple story structure. The story held up several plots which are interdependent on the other and one cannot occur without the other happening. It's perfectly alright to repeat, however much more could have been done to intensify the subplots. For example, I would have loved that at a crucial moment, it is Leia who displayed the art of 'this are not the droids you're looking for'. I would also have preferred that audience aren't let in first on the reason why Solo will have a secret solo mission on his own, which is to distract his son. So many could-haves.. but all has beens.

It was amazing back then, when one gradually discovered how Lucas mimed the entire Nazi machinery on-screen into science fiction. From the misnomer 'Stormtroopers', to their military structure and uniforms. Now, barely anything in the story is anywhere near inspiring. Hollywood has forgotten how to portray evil much less good.

With the reportoire of works that he has had, there's no reason for Abram's sub-standard treatment of this story of old. He didn't even try. But he's done it now, rounding off the last set of the trilogy by making it nothing more then a hodge podge series of stories about father-killers. Either the idiot be him, or he's actually a flexible genius to not have Michael Bay-ed every show he directs. Because if anything, this latest piece of work could be a secret parody directed at the dearth of cinematic imagination and how poor audience expectations actually controls the direction of the Star Wars mythos. He at least effectively used the opening scenes of fallen Republic war machines to signify the detachment of the new series to the original stories many were once familiar with. It's a tough job because we must remember that there are varied segments of audiences. Those that missed all the episodes before, those that experienced the second series but not the first. And those in their 30s and 40s who were there since the genesis. On top of these, what was fascinating before may have fallen short because of what's currently hogging audience's and critics' interests. But regardless of these varied considerations, what is core to the business of cinematic magic shldn't have change. Therefore, I would still consider unforgivable that he has dropped the entire franchise into an abyss of uncertainty.

Verdict: 1 out of 5 stars. Nothing remotely redeeming. Mentioned spoilers at the start but I assure you, there's not much more damage I can do from what it has already done to itself.

title: Hackneyed Plot Ruins Much Anticipated Movie
review:
If you are a Star Wars devotee, I anticipate that you will wish to skip this review.

Conversely, if you are someone who wants to read a review devoid of gratuitous praise, please read on.

I must first state that I wanted to enjoy this movie. However, an overwhelming sense of déjà vu (no, not nostalgia) prevented me from immersing myself in the experience. Sadly, the plot of this movie was hastily cobbled together from the original trilogy. For example, the climax of 'The Force Awakens' occurs when yet another death star is destroyed (granted, this one comes with a picturesque, wintry landscape that would make even Austria envious – I believe this was done so that the new villain, Kylo Ren, can work on his snowboarding skills. While this is conjecture, it is the only plausible reason to explain why this death star has been made to look like the idyllic picture on the front of a package of hot chocolate). Moreover, after thirty years, haven't the bad guys learned their lesson? Why have they not refrained from making planetoids with conveniently placed orifices that allow penetration by the X-wing Starfighters each and every time? In addition, this new contraption has the ability to drain the energy from a star until it disappears, which in and of itself is devastating. Indeed, if our sun were to wink out of existence, we would not know about it for approximately 8 & ½ minutes before, cloaked in a mantle of eternal darkness, we sailed off into oblivion. Thus, it is not necessary to pulverize a planet when it, too, would suffer a similar fate after its parent star was snuffed out. But what is eternal darkness when compared to the razzle-dazzle of Hollywood special effects and light shows (although, truth be told, watching a red line meander across the screen is not that exciting – but that's probably just me). Imagine, for a moment, a scene that showed the look of horror on the faces of the citizens on the daylight side of the planet as light from the sun vanished, and, on the night side of the planet, light from a moon suddenly winks out while familiar stars in the sky (light reflected from other planets in the system) also faded from view. This could have been used to great effect.

Setting aside the hackneyed plot, I must express my disappointment with the casting of the new generation of Star Wars actors. Rey (Daisy Ridley), the new Luke Skywalker (another hero from a desert environment who is filled to the brim with the force and just waiting for the right mentorship) wears a constant expression on her face that can only be described as "I'm running late for my Pilates class!" It was a static performance, and there was nothing beyond her humble circumstances that encouraged me to sympathize with her. Next, I was unnerved watching an unmasked Kylo Ren (Adam Driver), in yet another bridge scene, because it clearly looked like he had been cast in a biopic about Frédéric Chopin and had stumbled onto the Star Wars set by mistake. I fear that Finn (John Boyega) was out of his depth because his demeanor came across like a tourist visiting a 'Stars Wars Adventure' at theme park that includes standing in front of a green screen and acting out a two-minute scene. As his involvement required much more than two minutes, his self-consciousness became uncomfortably apparent. Two important exceptions were the new droid, BB-8, which fit nicely into the Star Wars universe (Abrams is to be commended for not letting this character upstage its human counterparts) and Maz Kanata, who was voiced by Lupita Nyong'o – this character brought much needed freshness to the storyline and was a true respite from the tired, recycled material foisted on the audience for most of the movie. The writers also made the cardinal sin of assuming a relationship between the new characters that the audience is not allowed to see develop. For instance, Finn and Poe Dameron (Oscar Isaac) meet briefly before stealing a Twin Ion Spaceship and crash landing on the planet Jakku where they immediately lose track of one another. When the two characters meet up later in the movie for the "let's destroy the death star" scene, Poe greets Finn like a long-lost brother, which strains credulity given that they have only just met and spent mere minutes together before being separated.

While it was gratifying to see the veterans again, with the exception of Han Solo (Harrison Ford), their appearance was both obligatory and forced. Gone was the Leia/Solo banter that made the original movies so charming. C3POs brief cameo, with a red arm, was as baffling as it was unnecessary.

I believe that all of the positive buzz may be chalked up to another instance of the 'Emperor's New Clothing'. Consider that it was not the gullibility or the naiveté of the people of the fable that made them overlook a man who was naked; rather, it was how much they had invested in this man based on an underlying belief that he could only be dressed in the kingdom's finest garments. Similarly, devotees of the Star Wars franchise so desperately want to believe that a top notch movie has been produced that its palpable shortcomings have been knowingly overlooked. I do not regret seeing the movie; I do regret donating more money to the Walt Disney Company for a movie that contained very little original or engaging material.

title: It's the iPhone 6 of sequels
review:
Since the critic reviews had left me hopeful that something new and exciting was brewing with the Star Wars series, I felt disappointment as the final credits rolled in the theater. I'll drop it in easy point form.

The Bad: -The soundtrack. Please just calm down with the music. Are the scenes really that weak that they need constant orchestral support? -The entire story was taken from the recycling bin. All of it. Nothing was fresh. If you fed all of the Hollywood films, from 1970 to 2010, into a computer and told it to recombine them into a random 2 hour film, it would eventually come up with this exact story.

-I felt nothing. My heart rate stayed a steady 60 BPM for the entire film, I am certain.

-Sound in space? This is 2016! In the '70's people perhaps didn't know any better, but in 2016 even children know that sound isn't transmitted in a vacuum. Please just give it up already.

-Robots that speak in bleeps. Come on! It would be a trivial matter for a robot maker to install speech capability, even if that robot had been made in 2010, let alone in... 2300 or whenever this movie supposedly takes place. We had R2D2 and that was enough. He was cute, we get it, but you've already used it up and now it's time to move on.

-An ex good guy now a bad guy controlled by an evil overlord. Perhaps the writers aren't fans of books, because if they were they would realize that they can do something more imaginative.

-The list is ending here, but know that I was SMH throughout the entire movie.

The good (there was some!): +Han Solo died (at least he was still dead at the end). Yes, this is good. It means that the writers have decided to move on with something. Even if he was pretty much the only saving grace of the series. Really, Star Wars needs to kill of main characters more often. It has become like a Marvel series where we don't even worry if the main character is in a bind because we know with 100% certainty that we will survive.

+CG and special effects. These have come a long way. Some people involved in this film know their jobs well. They weren't over done and they didn't take away from the story (ha). Kudos to the special effects people.

+The converted Storm Trooper. Hey, that was different. Something was different! I started by rating this 5/10 but after writing this review I've realized it should only be a 4/10.

title: A long time ago in a bank account far far away......The Shareholders Awaken
review:
if I could register a negative score I would.

BB8 and chewie the two non speaking characters have the best lines in the film. Okay sarcastic joke, but that emphasises the lack of quiet action from the real protagonists. The dialogue was simply not there, the plots so paper thin and written for a pre pubescent teen audience of the 21st century. I watched Episode IV aged about 6 in the cinema. Our family went back to see it again. The draw was the performances, the action, the plot, subplot arcs, the visuals, nothing was left to chance, no meaningless scenes. There was nothing with which this film could be compared. One came away from A New Hope wanting to be a Jedi and learn the ways of the force. Alec Guiness informed us it was all around us, it bound the galaxy together. I fell in love with Star Wars, did you hear that Disney!

Roll on the 21st Century McDonald's we are rewarded with insta Jedi. Rey doesn't need to learn the force. Having never heard of it in the first third of the film, but by minute 99 she is a fully fledged mind reading, sabre wielding Jedi master. I seem to remember Luke not being able to raise his X-wing on Dagoba. Luke staring on as Ben tricks a sand trooper in Mos Eisley. But Rey is able to trick a Stormtrooper like Ben because she needs to escape to further the plot. Jedi instant it seems just add water must!

That's what you get a watered down version of a film they used to call Star Wars. If you took away the action scenes, which weren't memorable, took away the music, which they did by the way and were left with just the dialogue, you'd be left with a really threadbare stage play. No character development, plots which don't knit together, no plot arcs, sub plot or character involvement/ compassion. Can anyone tell me anything about Poe? The character is a blank, as is Max Von Sydow, Rey, Phasma. Finn is the most confusing a pacifist who loves to kill Stormtroopers? Followed by Ren a dark Jedi who apparently didn't need the mask, just a deeper voice! Vader's mask was a life support. Ren has a toy mask pretending to be Vader. A fake mask for a fake character.

Why wasn't Ren disfigured? This was one of countless and I mean countless plot fails and character defects which plagued the film from start to end.

BB8 didn't need to carry the map, unlike R2, he didn't need to be delivered safely. Why was there a map in the first place, I still have no idea what that plot entails? Who hides but thinks to leave a map? The Falcon was lost or stolen? No one scavenged the Falcon in a town full of scavengers? Poe and Finn are instantly best friends and trust each other despite being from opposite camps. Did the director not watch Ice Cold in Alex? Ren shot by a wookie despite being able to stop laser blasts mid air? Then loses to a novice Jedi, I use that term novice for Rey, she wasn't even an apprentice Jedi! Everyone can wield a light sabre at the first attempt. Remember how clumsy Luke was on the Falcon in Episode IV, then trained with Yoda, then lost to Vader in Empire, then barely beat Vader in ROTJ.

REY IS BY THAT EQUATION BETTER THAN YODA!

A starving Rey doesn't sell the droid for food. Chased by clean looking Stormtroopers in a dusty backwater minutes after finding the droid. Can fly the Falcon at first attempt. Not even Luke flew the Falcon, EVER! Can repair the Falcon as well, making Han and Chewie out to be amateurs in their own ship. Why wasn't Han rewarded after helping to save the Galaxy risking his life over three films, no he has to go back to smuggling? No fear he finds his beloved legendary ship, which no one recognised, but they still seem to know about the Kessel Run incident, 14 sorry12 parsecs, cue canned laughter.

Han finds the Falcon milliseconds after it left the planet floor of Jakku? Yet he cannot locate Luke?

Hux shouts at his troops, not really an Imperial Commander, Ren trashes his computer games consol. Tries often in repeated scenes to use Jedi mind tricks to draw information from his enemies. Runs around after said enemies trying to locate a droid, Vader would have delegated that responsibility. Isn't that what Bounty Hunters are for? Every pub has a spy and instantly recognises the droid and calls it in to the First Order, who are they? Never explained. Not the Empire as this would have died with its EMPEROR!

Luke's incorrect light sabre from Empire, the one he lost, found in a box in a basement at Yellow sorry Orange Yoda's pub.

....and so it goes on.

Han dies and no one blinked or cried. When he was encased in carbonite who didn't have a lump in their throat? The minute he walked on the bridge we all knew what was coming, what a postcard ending.

An amateurish, plot stealing attempt from A New Hope being passed off as a new film. It is at best a rough homage.

We should be asking for our money back and a remake.

A sad end to the Star Wars saga and the films I used to love.

Goodbye Han.

It's crap all of it!

title: Really just a 2nd rate plodding reboot
review:
The original Star Wars trilogy didn't amaze on plot lines, didn't amaze on dialogue, didn't amaze on ideas. But they did have genuine on screen chemistry and a sense of wide eyed wonder provided by the directors and actors. Even with the prequel trilogy the directing and acting at least felt connected (although too often infantilized) to the original trilogy. And the stories showed they were made by people familiar with the original trilogy.

But this?

First, as many other reviewers have noted, the plot simply doesn't make sense after the ending of episode VI. It feels simply like a slightly remixed remake reboot. Now, if Star Wars had been only moderately successful and rarely repeated then fine, this approach may have been worthwhile. But this is Star Wars! The most widely known films of all. So what were the creators thinking? If they'd gone even more infantile then OK, maybe it would be a reboot for the very young, too young to have watched the originals. But they didn't. They went more aggressive, so if anything for older viewers than the original. It simply doesn't make any sense, let along the US$millions of sense it took to make.

Second, regardless of this, it is simply a weak film, lacking in motivations, consequences or any snappy chemistry, save for one 5 second piece toward the end of the film.

The only redeeming features are the special effects (but anyone can do this now) and art direction, but even that is simply decent rather than good.

I gave this a view after wasting 2 and a quarter hours on Rogue One and thinking surely no, the good reviews for Ep VII must mean something. I was mistaken.

I liked the idea of a defecting stormtrooper and I like the new Jedi girl. However the film was spoilt by too many repeating themes...a new and bigger death star? Really? A son/father, one dark side, one good? An old, wrinkly looking alien (like Yoda) who seems to know everything? The Empire basically renamed as The First order. It felt as though the writers felt they had to do almost a remake of the very first film just to get younger viewers up to speed. Why do they seem to have gone backwards in 30 years? Why has Han's and Leia's son gone to the dark side and why aren't they together? It was spoilt even more when Kylo Ren took his mask off..he just looked like some haughty student. He just was not scary any more. Spoiler: and when Kylo Ren killed his father it just seemed so unnecessary and meaningless. Did the writers just think oh yeah we will make it like the opposite of when Luke fights his father. title: Competent but derivative reboot of American exceptionalism undermined by crucial miscast of storm trooper character
review:
Star Wars: The Force Awakens is the 7th installment in the great money-making pantheon. After Disney bought out George Lucas, the progenitor of the series, the decision was made to conscript the heavily Spielberg influenced director, J.J. Abrams, who agreed to direct a veritable clone of Episodes 1 through 3 (eschewing the "dark" prequels of Lucas' Episodes 4 through 6). The three original episodes represented a grand updating of the old movie serials of the 30s and 40s, particularly those produced by Republic Pictures, known for outstanding special effects.

Even more influential is the memory of America's last "noble" conflict: World War II. Indeed, The Force Awakens (TFA) features villains primarily modeled on Nazi Germany and to a lesser extent, fascist Imperial Japan. In TFA, the Nazis take the form of "The First Order," sounding very similar to the Nazis' "new order" (the political order which Nazi Germany wanted to impose on the conquered areas under its dominion). The Star Wars' "good guys" are part of the "Resistance," a moniker usually reserved for the French, who battled the Germans on their own turf in World War II. First Order Stormtroopers appear to be a stand-in for the Waffen SS (militarized formations of Hitler's elite bodyguards and special police force), who commit Nazi-like atrocities, eliminating innocent inhabitants on the planet Jakku. The mysterious Supreme leader Snoke harks back to the image of Emperor Hirohito, an inscrutable figure in the eyes of many Americans during the second World War.

TFA features the derring-do of fighter pilots who look and sound like Americans. "Alien" pilots are also part of the Resistance and they represent foreign nationals who assisted the Americans and the British in the air campaign against Nazi Germany and Japan. American Harrison Ford as the smuggler Han Solo and one of the new protagonists, Brit Daisy Ridley, as the scavenger Rey, exemplify any civilian (on either side of the Atlantic), who assisted in the war effort (Rey's capture and subsequent interrogation by the First Order peg her as a descendant of MI5 or OSS spies entrusted with secret information—in this case, Rey must not give away the crucial information of the map that will lead to the whereabouts of Luke Skywalker).

Additional World War II allies find their counterparts in TFA. Maz Kanata (voiced by Lupita Nyong'o) is the Yoda-like, ET looking alien who brings wise advice from what must be a timeless, magical Orient. And Max Von Sydow, a retired adventurer on the planet Jakku, undoubtedly typifies any ally from the Scandinavian countries that aided English-speaking combatants.

The TFA is seriously undermined by the politically correct casting choice of renegade Stormtrooper Finn played by John Boyega. Finn not only doesn't have a very good reason for going "rogue," but if the First Order believes in racial superiority like their Nazi counterparts, Finn would hardly be a candidate for inclusion in the elite Stormtrooper unit. Even if you buy the idea of Finn's change of allegiance, Boyega's decision to turn the character into a buffoon of sorts (replete with his cowardly decision to go AWOL), casts an amateurish pall on the TFA proceedings. Instead, a young Arnold Schwarznegger type would have been far more appropriate in the role. One very sagacious IMDb poster suggested that Oscar Issac who plays the crack fighter pilot, Poe, should have been cast as Finn and Boyega should have taken the role of Poe.

It's pretty pointless rehashing the TFA plot but suffice it to say much of what goes on is a rehash of what we've seen before in Episodes 1 through 3. BB8, the new "droid," is quite delightful as the roly-poly "pet" who belongs to Rey and hides part of the puzzle that will lead to Luke. Star Wars aficionados will probably dig the reappearance of the rundown Millennium Falcon ship but when Han Solo unleashes the cargo against criminals out to get him, the ensuing mayhem (featuring rapacious snake-like creatures) translates into what appear to be some rather bad outtakes from one of the Men in Black pictures. When the Falcon crew travels to the planet Takodana, there's more nostalgia as the camera pans through a cantina consisting of most of the cooler aliens in the Star Wars universe.

The hurried TFA climax is nothing to write home about. Particularly puerile is Rey's ability to use the Force to direct a Stormtrooper to unlock her restraints so she can escape. Then there's the rather predictable Oedipal confrontation between Kylo Ren and his dad, Han Solo. Guess who meets his demise? Finally, there's the rather pointless and dull light-saber battle first between Kylo and Finn and then Rey, who manages to get the better of the deranged psychopath.

Just like in the originals, the American (oops, I mean the Resistance) fighter pilots do their thing and destroy The First Order's base. I neglected to mention Princess Leia (now General Leia), played by the late Carrie Fisher. She unfortunately didn't have much to do except hug Han Solo and later get misty eyed over his death.

Mark Hamill has such a small part here that we can only hope the Star Wars scenarists come up with something a little more substantial for the iconic super hero, the next time around. Hamill unfortunately didn't have much of a career after starring in the original Star Wars—so he probably (and unfortunately) has the most to prove.

TFA might have been better if there was more of a focus on what made the bad guys tick. Instead, it's just another reboot of a reboot: the Star War Universe episodes 1 through 3, as a stand-in for American exceptionalism in World War II. Again, if you a Star Wars aficionado, you probably can't go wrong here. Others should be slightly wary.

title: Dear God, put the force back to sleep...
review:
...until a time when a halfway decent writer, director, actors, costume designer, set builders and music composer can be found. This movie was made for check-your-brain-at-the-door millennial bed-wetters, not for the more sophisticated movie-goer. It is a nostalgia movie and nothing more. Had this movie not been associated with Star Wars, it would've bombed at the box office and received overwhelmingly negative reviews much more akin to the recent Fantastic 4 movie.

As soon as I heard that Jar Jar Abrams was doing this updated Star Wars Holiday Special, I knew it was definitely not going to be good, but I wasn't expecting it to be this BAD. Jar Jar, still riding his fame for LOST, even though his only real involvement in that show was the pilot episode, has shown that he can completely beat to death time-honored franchises like Star Trek and flip the bird to its fans. The sets used in this movie made the original trilogy look state of the art in comparison. Every one of the costumes have a cheaply constructed fan-film quality to them. Kylo Ren's costume reminded me of Klytus from the 1980 Flash Gordon movie. As bad as the prequels were, you could still look forward to a cool light-saber duel, but even when that moment came in this new film, you were let down BIG TIME. From the very first shot, this movie made a concerted effort to copy the original Star Wars. The points made in every bad review reflected my exact thoughts. Every character in this movie is even more shallow and uninteresting as the prequel characters. Even the bad guys act silly and elicit about as much negative feelings towards them as the Nazis in the third Indiana Jones movie. If the entire First Order is looking for BB-8, as long as they don't need any cigarettes lit, why don't the main characters just leave this otherwise useless droid behind? I have my own theory about that. I believe that the soul of Jar Jar Binks was preserved in perpetuity inside the little droid. Hey, if you're going to make a parody version of a classic movie, why not go all out? Besides that, what happened to Carrie Fisher's voice? It doesn't go above a whisper and it sounds heavily slurred. She sounded just like that lady in the anti-smoking ads with the stoma in her neck. Chewie didn't even look like Chewie anymore but rather a Wookiee that had just walked out of a hair salon.

There are bad movies and there are movies that are so bad, they leave you in a lousy mood for the rest of the day. This movie is the latter. After watching this, I found it much more entertaining and cathartic to read all the negative reviews. If you hated this movie, the best thing you can do to express your anger is to boycott any more Star Wars movies and merchandise.

title: What a waste of Time & Money
review:
This is my first and only ever review. Big Fan of IMDb, but i wanted my say, because i thought finally we were going to get a movie befitting a continuation of the original story line.

I realise we all have different views, ideas, perception etc and so i mean no disrespect to anyone. So this is just my opinion, someone at an age that just couldn't wait for this movie to come out (BFI IMAX), knew that JJ was at the helm (after his wonderful reboot of Star Trek) and was expecting a spectacular continuation, as this i thought was his opportunity to tell a story like George Lucas did in 1977, without the hardships and stress that George went through.

Unfortunately i can't give this a zero.

First i want to apologise, as i can't express my major disappointment, without a couple of spoilers. I won't go through the whole movie, just a couple of a major points that put the nails in the coffin for me.

You've seen "A New Hope", then you've seen this movie, just a poorer version. No originality, No imagination, No addictive storyline and what a poor anti-climax. Very poor casting, hey!, why don't we do what we did in the Pirates of the Caribbean ? cast a good looking English girl!

Daisy Ridley is very pretty and was actually not bad in this Garbage, so i give the mark of "1" to her.

"""" SPOILER ALERT """"

The two things that killed this movie for me:

1) You Killed Han Solo, you killed STAR WARS !!!!

2) Someone please tell me! how the offspring of Han Solo and Leia Organa be so ugly, with a big nose.

$200m dollars on absolute Garbage!!!!!!

I could have written a better storyline\sequel, that i am sure off.

I would like to apologise to George Lucas for not giving him the credit his prequels deserved and seeing them for what they were. You at least had imagination and originality all the way through.

Long Live George Lucas!!!!

My punishment!!! I have paid for two more screenings of this Garbage - a total of £225 wasted personally and in the kitty of Walt Disney.

title: I don't like what this film is doing to Star Wars.
review:
Return of the Jedi had a solid ending and to continue this story you have to do better than (spoiler alert) give us no context in A New Hope Reboot that just happens to say Episode VII The force Awakens.

There aren't any planets we haven't seen before. Jakku is Tatooine with war machines that crash landed on it's surface.

(Spoiler Alert) A Coruscant TYPE planet get's destroyed along with 5 other planets with the Death Star 3 that takes energy from the sun. It get's blown up in the same way. All of our hero's efforts in the Original Trilogy is undone.

The effort of our heroes being undone would be more acceptable if the enemy was completely different from the one in the OT. Another power arising as a threat would have been fine.

(Spoiler alert) The point of the Prequels was to show how a war get's started and how power can be brought into the wrong hands by war. The Phantom Menace starts out with everything being fine and by ROTS everything goes downhill.

Here everything goes downhill from a time where we are lead to think everything would be fine.

If this was a different story I could accept this but it's not. I thought it was better than Attack of the Clones objectively. What get's me is they treated the movie like almost all ideas in the Prequels were terrible so don't have ideas. Don't try to expand the universe. (Sarcasm) It's not like Star Wars has endless potential or anything right? It's just the same thing over and over again.

The Prequels made me expect too much I suppose. I mean we got Georges creative mind behind everything. We got PodRacing, Gungans (they're awesome forget about the overused character Jar Jar for a second), A giant war between what seems to be 2 disposable armies but it makes for some amazing footage, seeing what it means when Obi Wan told Luke your eyes can deceive you don't trust them with the saber fights, and the overall result ending with despair but a glimmer of hope.

I felt like this film made the Original Trilogy look bad in making it completely irrelevant.

Were there mistakes made with the prequels, well, yes but no one properly learned from them. Georges ideas with script doctoring and good execution that's how you do STAR WARS! That is how the Force works!

I "Hope" Rouge One is stronger with it! They need a film to distract from this last one for a while.

review:

title: A forceful awakening...
review:
Watched the movie twice.I really tried to like it and find something at least half great as the advertising campaign behind it.

The story might keep you interested although it's a recycled one.Its connections and references to the old movies take the spotlight in front of the narration.Sadly, this movie is not about its story.

It's about its characters. Sadly(again), its characters are very weak in their construction.I understand that some of them can have a weak back story,or no back story at all but when you have a movie like this one on your hands though,you need to treat your characters with more respect.And your audience.Some of us are not willing to wait for another movie to find out who are they. No glimpse of their past,their motivation or purpose.Everything the two main characters do is forced out of their nature and context.The only one that is believable is the antagonist. He is the only one that has a clear reason to be in this movie and he seems quite determined to show it. He gets his motivation from Vader, whom he admires and reaches out to. We don't know all of his back story, but we understand that he was not like that from the beginning.You won't get an explanation for the strange light-saber from the trailer though.

I'm sure everybody likes the music from Star Wars.I was glad to find out they got the same John Williams to do the soundtrack.In the theater I was disappointed to hear music on 85% of the movie.Excess is a trademark of bad taste.The music is very good, but it was too much for me and it had an unexpected effect.During one battle on a planet, there is no music.The sound design from that sequence might not be that bad, but when you play music from frame one till the end and leave a moment like that not covered by Williams,that moment seems much more weaker and the sound design really poor. I understood why they did it that way.It marks a moment when a character sees the other(at least for a long time), but doing it like this shows that Jar-Jar Abrams is a mediocre film school student director at best. There are more appealing ways to treat a moment like that one.He chose the least creative one and the safest way.Overall the movie is a safe-bet.People will like it although it's not groundbreaking.It's not even going in a slightly different direction.

Star Wars has some good moments.I won't take those away from the movie.I enjoyed the action sequences.Fast paced editing, lots of tension and twists.They seem a bit singular in the whole context but they worked.The thing that bugged me were the jokes...the Disney Effect.I did not feel in the mood for small humor in a Star Wars movie.Han Solo made jokes in the old movies,but it was part of his character.Here, everybody has a small moment of cheap humor.Instant turn off.

I don't know what I expected from a Star Wars movie directed by Abrams(several of his trademarks are here).I don't like his movies,and I'm sure that whatever I wanted from this movie, I did not get it.

Just don't expect to see a masterpiece.

title: The Farce Awakens
review:
 The story really moved, almost too fast at times, and resembled the Star Trek movies.  I thought there were way too many coincidences, which IMO was a pre-existing weak element of the other films. Force Awakens took it and ran.  Given the fact that the Empire and the Sith are still there really diminishes the ending to ROTJ and fully qualifies Episode VII thru IX as simply add-on sequels in my mind.  The middle of the film sagged quite a bit, similar to ROTJ. I'm referring to many of the scenes on Yavin and the plan to destroy the super weapon. I cringed during exposition dialogue between Han and Leia. Are they really going to sum up why they've been separated from each other after so many years in a sentence or two and now everything is just peachy? Wasn't buying it.  Speaking of dialogue, I suppose people prefer a healthy "YEAH!" and "WOOO!" to "Yipee!". I don't see a huge difference.  I thought the scene where Finn and Rey turned to the Falcon, revealing the ship (and direct link to the OT for the first time) was cool.  The person I attended with thought there was too much humor in the movie. I did enjoy some of it, but I think it may have been a bit much at times. I think this movie probably had more humor moments than any from the OT, which is probably too much.  I liked some of Han Solo's scene, and the exchanges with Finn were humorous. Other times he seemed like an old goof. I liken it to the way Kevin Anderson wrote the character versus Timothy Zahn in the post-ROTJ era novels. I prefer Zahn, and I didn't see much of that here.  Wasn't buying the sudden obsession that Finn had to save Rey. I could easily see this as a budding romance in the upcoming sequels. That's the only motivation I could reason.  I thought Daisy Ridley did a nice job, but I'm not sold on the central character and heir of this franchise being a woman in what's traditionally been a mostly male fanboy set of war movies set in space. I know some will think that's a sexist remark, however, I think those people are confusing art with social and political standards in our society. If Disney is trying to expand their target audience to include a large majority of women, then just come out and say so instead of pretending that Lucas did something wrong or times have changed. It's insulting to the original fans.  Adam Driver's character was interesting and complex. I welcomed the scenes where he took off the mask.  I liked Poe Dameron based on his limited screen time.  BB-8 was a likable character.  Captain Phasma - meh  Snoke struck me as a giant Gollum or something out of Harry Potter. Not much originality.  Rey and certainly Finn appeared to have acquired dueling techniques a little too quick for my taste, especially when matched against Kylo Ren, who obviously was dedicated to the task.  This movie marks the fourth out of seven where the climax revolves around a super weapon being destroyed. Do people think that's a requirement for a movie to "feel" like SW?  Not much fuss was kicked up around Han Solo's death after it happened. Nobody consoled Chewie and he seemed to bounce back rather quickly. At least Padme got a funeral.  R2-D2 on the other hand was completely distraught and shuts down for years after a bunch of padawans were killed. I would think R2 would bounce back much quicker than Chewie, especially considering we lost HAN SOLO instead of characters that never had any screen time.  Powerful ending with Rey offering the lightsaber to a much older Luke. Leaves you wondering what's he thinking? I'm not sure I want to see more. Some things are better left untold :)

I think ANH, ESB, ROTJ and ROTS were better movies. Not sure where I would rank this one with the rest yet...

title: A Poor Remake Of A New Hope.
review:
Like so many I am a massive fan of the original 3 movies and although the prequels didn't measure up to the first 3, they did stand on their own in terms of story line and character building, but The Force Awakens was, I have to say a real disappointment. With J.J Abrams, Disney's budget, the original movies writers all involved in the project there was so much hope for this movie, but at the end of it you realise the only hope was a poor politically correct remake of the original A New Hope.

Spoilers below. The Empire has re-emerged but is now called the "First Order". The Rebels are no longer the rebels but are now the "resistance". There is a new Death Star, only this one is called the Star Killer Base, to add to the lack of imagination the weapon they use to wipe out planets is called "the weapon".

Almost from the opening scene we are set for a rerun of Star Wars episode IV, instead of a woman loading up the plans into a droid, as Leia did in the first one, we have a guy called Poe, who has a map with the whereabouts of Luke Skywalker. The droid escapes the ship with the map, just before it gets boarded by the Empire, sorry "First Order" and lands on a Tatooinesque planet, where the droid finds its way to "Rey" who is the female version of Luke Skywalker from the original.

Kylo Ren played (poorly) by Adam Driver is our new "Vader", he wears a mask to distort his voice for no other reason then to wear a mask to distort his voice.

In the original, Darth Vader needed his mask to regulate his breathing because of the injuries he had sustained with his final battle with Obi Wan, but Kylo wears it as a fashion accessory to make him look the part of the villain.

He plays the conflicted ex pupil of Skywalker, who has been seduced by the "Dark Side". He is completely unbelievable as the Dark Lord, no where near as menacing as Darth Vader and he plays the part like a rebellious teenager with daddy issues who likes a mask.

He then "hunts down and kills his father", who happens to be Han Solo taken straight from the New Hope scene when Luke meets Obi Wan for the first time and Obi Wan tells him how a young Jedi he trained turned to the dark side hunted down and killed Anakin. The way Han Solo is killed, by Ren (also called "Ben" by Solo) meet on the new Death Star / Star killer base, is almost an identical way as when Darth killed Obi Wan.

There are far many more similarities to A New Hope, from going onto the Star Killer base to rescue Rey from Ren, having to lower the shield so the rebellion, sorry resistance, can blow up the Death Star, oops, I mean Star Killer Base.

Domhnall Gleeson who plays General Hux is so over acted and completely unbelievable that it makes you wonder how he even got the role. Peter Cushing, who played the part of Grand Moff Tarkin in the original, played the part with class. He was cool, calm and collected and very believable as the head of a powerful battle station, the complete opposite of General Hux who seems to want to throw a tantrum in every scene.

On top of all the bad acting, poor remake attempt of the New Hope, we have the typical Disney political correctness loaded in to the movie.

We have the "Black Stormtrooper" who is the only good one and refuses to kill all the villagers.

Rey a woman, has now taken on the Luke Skywalker role.

You can obviously see where Disney is going with this, "Rey" will probably end up being "Rens" sister, she will be hunted down by Snook, who is the new emperor, he looked like one of the Orcs from lord of the rings if you ask me. Snook will no doubt either try and turn Rey to the dark side, she will probably find out Leia is her mother, only to be saved by "Finn" the storm trooper who is no longer a storm trooper and Ren will probably kill Snook, when he comes to terms with his conflict of the dark side and returns to the good side of the force.

Female heroine, black hero, hunted by the over acted villainous white male, all they did was try to politically correct the old version to fit in with Hollywood's agenda.

The plot is rushed and has so many holes, there is zero character development, that we have absolutely no idea where "Snook" came from, how the "First Order" came to exist, how they were able to build a massive storm trooper army and how they have all the Empire ships.

This was a great opportunity for a great movie, to pick up after the Return of the Jedi. There were so many more roads they could have gone down, considering this was no longer a prequel they had an open script to play with, but instead they chose to redo the original with an agenda.

Why Hollywood keep messing with originals and trying to remake classics to fit with todays agenda is beyond me. The original 3 were great movies because they were movies made for movie goers, The Force Awakens is a movie trying to deliver a politically correct message dressed up in a remake of a cinema classic, then its aimed at movie goers.

Hollywood needs to stop with the political correctness and go back to doing what Hollywood should be doing and making movies for movie goers and leave the politics to politicians.
