title: A return to form, but it could of been so much more...
review:
Let me start by saying that I am a huge Star Wars fan. Ever since a kid I have been completely captured by the wonder of the SW universe, whether that be with the films, the novels, the games, you name it...

I was bursting at the seams to go and see this film and had such huge expectations for it (which perhaps done a disservice to the film).

It was good. I don't think it was terrible as others have said, but I don't think it was an "instant classic" or "masterpiece". It was simply a good film.

Visually the film was phenomenal. The action scenes were intense and extremely fast paced which came as a bit of a surprise to me. However, it was a kind of fast paced that you could actually follow and not feel completely lost whilst watching it. The characters and the chemistry between them felt a lot more natural as opposed to the previous entries.

However, I have two significant complaints about the direction they took with this film. Firstly, and I don't mean to jump on the bandwagon here, the film's plot is a carbon copy of ANH mixed in with elements from ESB and RotJ. I can understand perhaps JJ Abrams wanting to pay homage to the original films and give a nostalgia factor for the fans, but given that this film is set in a completely unexplored time period and the fact that it is independent of the Expanded Universe, I don't get why a completely new and original plot wasn't used. It was almost embarrassing at times how identical the film was to ANH (sand planet, hero stranded on the planet, droid with desperately needed information, Death Start mark 3, rescue protagonist from Death Star, X-Wings fly through trench and blow up super weapon from inside... you see where I'm going).

Additionally, I didn't like how trivial the force was portrayed. I think this is best reflected by the fact that Rey one minute is completely unaware of the fact she is force sensitive (even as far as believing that the Jedi and force were a myth) and the next she is using Jedi mind-tricks expertly - how did she even know that was a thing that was doable?!

All in all, I left the cinema feeling slightly disappointed, but still optimistic for the next two instalments. I just hope they go for something completely original. I don't mind the odd throwback here and there, but sometimes it can be way too much and even pointless... *cough* C3PO and Leia *cough*

title: The Force Awakens...A New Hope?!
review:
"Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery but also the clearest expression of mediocrity". Yep someone said that somewhere...can't remember who or where, but they do deserve credit, because in a way it perfectly encompasses the case of Jar Jar Abrams and "Star Wars Episode VII The Force Awakens" and his overlords at Darth Disney.

Jar Jar Abrams did what was exactly expected of him. Restart the "Star Wars" franchise, now under the Disney banner, and justify their $4 billion dollar purchase of Lucasfilm, without stumbling out of the starting gate. That he achieved.

Let me also say, that I never hated the Prequel Trilogy, and rather enjoyed the movies, imperfect though they were, except Jar Jar Binks (not to be confused with Jar Jar Abrams!)...that guy should be murdered and then cooked into a delicious meal of frog legs or whatever...but I will not be comparing those movies with this one!

Personally, and this makes it clear how subjective all these reviews are, I found "The Force Awakens" to be on OK, decent, alright flick. I was not overwhelmed by it. It is not a masterpiece, but neither was I underwhelmed, I do not hate the movie, despise it or anything of the sort.

Abrams has been an astute and observant student of the George Lucas and Steven Spielberg school of movie-making. Many of his projects, especially the cinematic ones, have been almost love letters to them. And such is the case with "The Force Awakens". It is a tribute from Abrams, as a fan, to the people and times which influenced and pushed him to become a movie maker.

Abrams is a technically adept director, but in his imitation-is-flattery type of movie-making also lies his mediocrity as I was alluding to in the opening line. That lack of a cinematic identity has unfortunately and oftentimes marked him as a director for hire, as in this instance here, with Disney and Abram's involvement with "Star Wars" (and other projects as well).

And therein lies perhaps the greatest weakness in "The Force Awakens", this smattering of mediocrity, it is a movie steeped in nostalgia, at some points so much so, that it feels like less of a new beginning and more like a re-boot or remake of "A New Hope"...or even worse, a carbon copy.

It is very clear that Darth Disney wasn't going to screw around with its newest acquisition slash golden goose, Lucasfilm. As I said, this is a safe movie at the hands of a safe director, who can create carbon copies and perfect replicas of Lucas and Spielberg's movies, but who lacks a vision and style of his own.

One of the things I like most about the movie, were the new casting additions to the franchise. Oscar Isaac, one of my favourite actors, goes without saying, but also John Boyega and Daisy Ridley. To me she is the heart and soul of the movie. It will be interesting to see how her story arc will develop. Plus Daisy Ridley is just lovely. They inject much needed life in this franchise.

Lets see what Rian Johnson and Colin Trevorrow will do. I think and hope, Rian Johnson will do a good job. Less certain about Colin Trevorrow, though I enjoyed "Safety Not Guaranteed" (I really wish we could get Doug Lyman to direct Episode IX"Edge Of Tomorrow" was outstanding).

title: As Dom DeLuise's said for Melbrooks "Nice, not thrilling, but nice". But still, I liked it. A lot!
review:
Pre-Scriptum: always read reviews after watching the movie. Read reviews only if you don't intend to watch the movie)

These days, I judge a movie by my sleep time. If I fall asleep, it's not that good. Like Spectre. I did not sleep in TFA. In terms of comparability, TNH to ROTJ cannot be split up and liked independently. I liked the whole middle trilogy, just like I like LOTR (even though some parts were somewhat slow).

Let me tell you what I like about Star Wars. The story line is actually OK. Rather simple. Kings and Queens, Prince and Princesses. A soap opera in a space setting. What really fascinated me were 2 things: the light sabre and Darth Vader (I became a fan of James Earl Jones since). The latter needs no review only r.e.s.p.e.c.t, but the light sabre  what a wondrous imagination! A simple extendible switchblade. In the words of OB1 – "an elegant weapon for a civilized age" indeed. Coupled with the fact that it could deflect blaster shots towards the enemy makes for an excellent shield/counter-foil as well. I simply loved it! Now there is a buzz about the crystals forming the light sabre, be it Kunda stones or Kaiburr crystals, that they are attuned to the Force and to the light sabre bearer. A sword that speaks. How more Frostmourne or Melnibonic can this get!

On to the movie. I went into the movie with no expectations. It could not have been as bad as the first trilogy. I did not like it much (though in all honesty I was simply happy that Star Wars was back). It was too clean. Not gritty enough. Too sanitized. The plot was much better and thicker. The story line was not much complicated though. Ray Park rocked. Ian McDiarmid rocked. Playing the mentally sibilant pliant maneuverer. He showed the complexity of ruling a galaxy (much like Indian parliament, I guess). Hayden Christensen was the other end of the spectrum. End of review for Hayden. But long and short, middle trilogy was far better than the first trilogy. What killed me softly and quietly like the hiss and rasp of a bad light sabre was the over use of the light sabres in the first trilogy. More does not mean good.

TFA was gritty. The visuals are a treat. The franchise having gone to Disney, kiddos were to be expected. Both on screen and as audience. Catch them young and make them pay. The story line is only just developing, so not much to be expected. The light sabre duels were raw. I agree it was like GOT fights. Hacking and slashing. No kendo, no finesse, but this can be explained away as to be polished in the subsequent episodes. If JJ (who is a genius) hacks away the coal block to a valuable stone and makes the light sabre sentient and polishes the light duels, I shall forgive him for everything. Even for making me feel like I was watching a Bollywood movie ripping off a Hollywood movie frame by excruciating frame in TFA. There are the usual shock and awe tactics, but nods and homages and hat tips should not swallow the usual gems and easter eggs. All in all, though it felt like a remake and a reboot to boot, it was a joyous experience for me to watch Star Wars on large screen again! Maybe not loved it, but I liked it and I well appreciate JJ's take. That's it for the movie review.

What I would have liked? Well, Hugo Weaving (who was considered) or Jeremy Irons (keeping the Scar voice of the Lion King) or a Morgan Freeman voice over as Kylo Rens. I want menace, if not, at least dripping evil. But alas, they are not Disney material. For mature audiences only. I cannot think of any youngsters who can hold a candle to any of the names above. I want classier light sabre duels, less gymnastics. Not more than 2 sabres, maybe max 3 in any given movie. Not like having hundreds of coloured tube lights on a South Asian wedding night. If they could make a movie on ewoks, surely they can make one on the light sabre with a deeper storyline; with Keanu Reeves starring!

title: A vast improvement to the sequels and a promising foundation for the next two films in the series.
review:
The Force Awakens provided an opportunity for me and for all Star Wars fans: a chance at redemption for a series that more recently left a bad taste in our mouths. Like most Star Wars fans I accepted that it could not live up to the originals, but went in begging for it to be better than the prequels; the result was somewhere in the middle.

Characters/ Acting

Rey (Daisey Ridley): Daisy Ridley's performance turned out to be one of the highlights of the film for me and yet another example of how effective a strong female character can be on the big screen. Rey is an interesting character because of all the complex issues surrounding her: her desire to know and be reunited with her family, her admiration for Han Solo who she looks up to as a clearly capable and like-wise to scale the innards of fallen star destroyers for equipment which she sells for food to survive. Rey is an interesting character because of all the complex issues surrounding her: her desire to know and be e tough individual, her struggles to understand her relationship with the force while at the same time wishing she could reject her greater role. In many ways her character is far superior to that of Luke in A New Hope, who I have always found a bit bland and somewhat whiny, if only because she is playing the roles of Luke and Han Solo simultaneously. Ridley performance reveals a spectrum of toughness, compassion, and wit that has me looking forward to her next role.

Finn (John Boyega): I cannot blame him for some of the terrible lines he was given in the film such as "Hell of a pilot" which were not only cheesy but were often unnatural to the context of his situation, but I can fault him for his delivery of these lines as well as many others. His facial expressions, his speech, and sometimes his lack of engagement when other characters were acting left me disappointed in his performance. While going into the film I was interested in getting to know Finn's character, by the end I was asking myself repeatedly "why is his character necessary to this film?" The more I consider Finn's character the more I wonder whether the filmmakers themselves knew what to do with his character. Like Rey, Finn tries to serve many functions at once: he is the C-3PO comic relief, the love/friend interest of Rey, the side of Solo that doesn't want to be a hero but just wants to run, and sometimes he is the hero or at least makes an effort to be. Unlike Rey's character though which is strengthened by all these complex characteristics which mesh well together, Finn's is pulled in many different directions that glaringly contradict. How is the audience supposed to reconcile the fact that sometimes he is the haphazard, comic relief often in need of rescue himself, such as when he is carried off by the creature in the ship and saved by Rey, while at other moments he is trying to be the hero and go into the Death Star to rescue Rey (only to actually contribute nothing to her rescue). While there are functions that he serves as far as advancing the plot, the melting-pot of personal traits given to Finn did not blend well and was not aided by the mediocre to sub-par acting skills of John Boyega.

Story/ Writing

As much as I would rather not compare Star Wars: The Force Awakens to Star Wars: A New Hope, the fact that this film is in many ways a retelling of the first Star Wars film requires me to do so. From the droid which escapes an imperial force with data critical to the rebellion right up to the destruction of yet another Death Star, this film is littered with not just references but borrowed ideas from the original. Even the characters themselves are in many ways an obvious recycling of the past: Luke is Yoda the wise teacher who has gone into solitude and must be sought out for training, Han is Obi-Wan the wise, old guide who is there to provide direction for the characters until they become self-reliant at which point he is killed by Kylo-Ren who in turn takes the place of Vader the ambitious former Jedi struggling with the inner turmoil between good and evil. The parallels are not subtly introduced but are readily apparent from each character's introduction.

I am conflicted by how to react to Abram's decision to make the film so much like A New Hope. On the one hand it makes the film very predictable. For example, once you realize that the film is essentially A New Hope you can begin searching for each character's equivalent and plugging them into the storyline; for example, once it became clear to me that Han was Obi-Wan, in my mind his fate was sealed. But then again I am conflicted because this is Star Wars not Inception or The Usual Suspects; we don't see Star Wars for its intricate plot. Return of the Jedi proved to us that we could see the same old story and still love it because it's Star Wars (just so long as it actually had a plot, and acting, and characters we cared about, unlike 3 movies which are undeserving of the title of Star WarsÂ…) Abram's intent, much like the newer Star Trek movies, was to give us the nostalgia we have been craving so badly and in this he succeeded. So while some will bemoan that another Death Star was destroyed or that the plot was predictable, this is an instance where that's fine by me.

Conclusion:

A vast improvement to the sequels and a promising foundation for the next two films in the series.

title: Decent popcorn movie. Better than the prequels, not Empire or Return.
review:
The Force Awakens marks the true return of the Star Wars saga. Packed with high visual effects, a cohesive story and a hard ending, this is a movie worth seeing in theatres.

This film is not without its faults.

The good:

The acting is good across the board. Sometimes Daisy Ridley and John Boyega come across as melodramatic or amateur, but Oscar Isaac, Adam Driver and the side players bring it, in a big bad way.

The visual effects and overall visual style are right on point, there are no unnecessary camera wobbles or JJ lens flares to be found, and the film is shot more practically than you might expect.

The screenplay is more or less solid.

The Not So Great:

This movie, for better or worse, is a back door remake of Episode IV. The plot points quite mirror those of Star Wars. You might say this is the Superman Returns of the Star Wars universe, whereas the Phantom Menace was the Superman IV of the franchise.

This movie is good, but there is a LOT of fanfare in here.

Why is Kylo Ren cos-playing as Darth Vader? This is truly never explained.

What are Han and Chewbacca's motivations?

A lot of characters do things that seem to be merely through backs to Episode IV? These are legitimate questions.

In some ways the prequels were more honest than The Force Awakens, in the sense that you understand why characters do the things they do, and this is coming from someone who is not a fan of the prequels,

Overall, I can't crap on this movie. It delivers on everything it promised, it's just a little too "fan-servicey" for me personally. I dare say that unlike something perhaps like Prometheus or Star Trek, The Force Awakens is less intellectually sophisticated than I would have liked, but that doesn't make it bad, it's just straight forward. It's not a thinking man's movie.

Cheers.

Next to that I expected the movie to be way darker, based on the trailers. They really tried to keep the Saga spirit and succeeded for 75%, but also missed some crucial points. Don't get me wrong, overall it was a highly enjoyable movie and it contained some great Star Wars elements (sometimes a bit too much copy), but I had expected a bit more...

title: more family drama than an episode of jerry springer
review:
The force awakens: more family drama than an episode of Jeremy Kyle. When Disney took over the Star Wars franchise in 2012 many feared that Disney would regurgitate an un-original, cheesy, money-maker trilogy, much like the prequels of the early noughties. Although there have been some serious improvements in the last decade or so, ultimately the force awakens lacks the charm and grit of the original trilogy.

Although when leaving the theatre, I thought it was an admiral shot on jj Abraham's part, the movie was on the whole lack-lustre, and yet it seems that my disappointment is relatively un-shared amongst the critic community. Or in simpler words: the critics have gone far too easy on the 7th instalment of franchise.

Here are my thoughts, warning- spoilers.

Having Adam driver cast as the bad guy, Kylo Ren, was nothing shy of genius. This character could have very easily fallen into the trap of being pantomime-esqe scary, which by some miracle has been avoided. Driver gives the dry-ness that modern audiences demand from their baddie. Think of the success of Christoph Waltz in Tarantino's 'Inglorious Basterds'- yes he is scary as all hell, but he doesn't just grunt and blow stuff up, there is depth to his character which is so often overlooked in similar films- this is the kind of villain that the modern audience expects. Kylo Ren ticks the box of being the scary guy in black that we know all too well in this series, with a little family drama to spice him up a bit, however my biggest frustration is that the mask he wears has no purpose other than to look all dark and brooding, so *ahem* what's the point of putting him in a mask?

Finn is one of the only characters who was saved from the cringe one-liners, and as a result was a refreshing addition to the film. Boyega is undeniably talented, and his character helps drive the film from just the family drama of the Skywalker clan, the downside of Finn is that he comes parcelled with rey, quite easily the worst character of the film. Ridley's performance was wooden at best, down-right irritating at worst, and although her shrieks of 'don't hold my hand' were made with the intentions of providing a plucky, independent female figure, ultimately her character doesn't develop enough to make a serious impact.

Oscar Isaac as Poe was surprisingly good, yes there was perhaps one too many brooding looks over the shoulder with the ominous "they're coming" and so on, but besides that, for the short while he was on screen Poe was enjoyable to watch. He is witty and charming and has a lot of potential, but the problem is that he is gone for the most of the movie. Isaac is incredibly talented, and his talent was lost in the film, but hopefully with the next instalment we will see a lot more of poe. What the film tries to do is remind us of the older characters we know and love, whilst at the same time giving us a group of people that feel that little bit different. Although you can spend hours debating who is Luke and who is Han solo, my theory is that the writers have split the fan favourite, Luke Skywalker, into the three characters. A Skywalker holy trinity if you will. We have the confidence and cool-ness in Poe, the moral drive and like ability in Finn, and the troubled backstory in Rey. Although there were a lot of good intentions, once again the film falls flat in trying to recreate the magic of the original trilogy, and perhaps without the novelty of Hamill, Fisher and Ford's appearances the film would have been a failure.

The plot is somewhat predictable, but this does not take away from the film, which is of course a family sci-fi adventure, not heavy Oscar-worthy drama. The main issue is that the writers are so much better than focussing on family drama surrounding Skywalker and co. they could have very easily stepped away from the whole father-son baddie vs. goodie combination and come up with something truly original. The film does fit well into the series, and is certainly not the worst instalment but as a stand-alone movie is nothing mind-blowing. Enjoyable, but I fear that without the big budget and huge history behind it, the film doesn't fill those big Star Wars boots.

Will I see the next film? Yes- but with lower expectations than I had hoped.

title: Good film but they told the wrong story.
review:
I never write reviews so this is my first. I was only inspired to write by the hugely negative and unfair reviews focusing on events not concerning the film. I don't care about the directors past works(people talking about star trek, wtf?), nor the other films or the possible future films, just the film in question.

I'll keep it short.

The film had great performances from everyone, cant fault them. Nice comedy, good rapport between characters and i did sincerely care for the them at the end and will look forward to what happens to them in the future.

Whats stops the film being great for me is the definite wrong focus on the main plot. To me, the main plot should have focused on Han Solo and Leia and Kylo Ren. After watching it i just felt that it was a sub plot and it felt as though but it had the emotional plot device in the film and was used to a negative effect. I understand that killing Han Solo was a powerful way to involve the characters and also the audience to make them invested in the future and give them a reason to fight and keep watching, it was a good move in IMO.

They could have dedicated a good 20-30 minutes of the film to delve into Leia and Han and the past 30 years and why we should care about Kylo Ren. It would have really built up a suitable ending for such a legendary character.

With this as the main plot, they could have still achieved what they did with the death star story and given a better introduction the newer characters and given them a good reason to care about the future.

The person who should have had the most adverse and emotionally charged reaction to Hans death was chewie. Not only was he there and watched Han die, but he has also spent all of the time i assume with Han in the past 30 years. Rey and Finn have only met Han for a small time and also didn't believe he existed and they act like he was their father whilst chewies response is largely glossed over.

It would have been great to have had chewie have an emotional showdown with kylo ren and we would have been completely gripped watching a wookie break down and go full beast. He could have dealt a good blow to kylo and been saved at the last minute for certain death by the newcomers and therefore given chewie a reason to identify with the new guys and also to drive home how important Han was to chewie.

Instead chewie gets a few head nods and sighs and within 15 minutes on screen he seems to be ready to go off on another adventure. They still could have had Finn and Rey split up and still pledge to see each other again and Rey was always going to see Luke in the end to develop her force. It wasn't very necessary for kylo to awaken it in her when that was clearly going to happen anyway in the future.

If they had focused on that instead of the death star, they could have capped off the history and explained the passage of time whilst letting the death star story do the setting up of the future, it would IMO have made the film stand on its own two legs. They also didn't include Leia in the kylo thing. It felt like it didn't mean very much to Leia which felt odd. Instead of a story of literal rebellions and empires, they could have had the heart breaking story of an estranged son rebelling and breaking his parents hearts only to commit patricide and give fuel to Leia's campaign not only as a resistance leader but as a grieving mother of a broken family.

It was a good film though but i just felt they got the plots in the wrong focus. I feel like such a powerful plot device should always be center stage, it would have really made this film something special, instead Han went out like a fart in the wind comparatively.

Now that Hans story has been told, they have squandered the opportunity to send him of right, a bit of wasted opportunity IMO.

I do however look forward to the next one.

title: Hope for the sequels, this one fell flat.
review:
SPOILER ALARM - DON'T KEEP READING IF YOU HAVEN'T SEEN IT*

I will give the movie a 7/10. I liked the starship battles, the cinematography, scenery and seeing Han & Chewie, Leia & Co. obviously made my heart jump.

But there are some things that keep that movie from being great and once the hype wears off, I think the rating on IMDb will go down and people (especially fans) will start to realize that there are some major flaws.

  • The new cast of characters (especially the villains) seem to be bland, like cameos without any depth and motivation


  • Kylo Ren is a wimp and there is no reason given for the things he does (including killing Han *snief*). He completely lacks emotional realism or a motive.


  • The heroes are not very iconic, I expected way more of Finn and Po. Especially Finn who is supposed to inspire a new generation of boys and give black kids something to look up to, falls short and ends up being just a dude without any talents or force powers, who picks up a lightsaber and gets his ass whopped hard, just to eventually end up in a coma.


  • Rey is OP. She is a better pilot than Po, a better mechanic and shot than Han and Finn. She also defeats a trained dark side user and uses force powers without any training and pretense. Wtf? Give females someone to vouch for yes, but please keep it real and don't let all the males look like whimps and fools. That was just ridiculous and smelled a little bit of right-wing feminism mentality (females > males)


  • The movie has dozens of Deus Ex Machina moments and plot holes. The biggest for me being that Luke goes into hiding for 30 years, let's Ben Solo go dark and isn't even there when one of his best friends dies. (Not to speak of not helping to stop the First Order destroy a whole star system and kill billions - dah)


  • This is probably the first time a soundtrack from John Williams falls short and sounds bland. I was really surprised by this. Not a single catchy new theme there.


I still have some hope that they will balance the main cast a bit in the sequels, give the villains some depth and not let Rey roll over everyone like it is a bad femnazi joke. And please let Luke do something else than just hang out in New Zealand and stare emo- surfer-beard style at Rey without saying a single word, that took me completely out of it.

title: Eco-friendly Star Wars: Successfully recycles both previous trilogies
review:
Rehashing Star Wars:

Â•Bigger badder Death Star absorbs stars and uses their energy to destroy planets

Â•The even more "old piece of garbage" Millennium Falcon

Â•Droid carries secret but vital information that changes the fate of the galaxy

Â•Orphan in a desert planet

Â•Main villain killing one hero, just in time for the others to see

Â•Main character falling to death in a chasm in the Death Star

Â•Main villain venting (EpII). This time Ren vents anger on computers, to remain politically correct.

Â•Same ending as EpIV: Group of starfighters assaults a heavily guarded trench on the surface of Starkiller Base to hit its vulnerable spot just seconds before it can destroy the Resistance's base. It even echoes the second Death Star and the ending of Episode I by having a starfighter enter the vulnerable point and attacking from the inside.

Â•An infant villain aspiring to be just like Darth Vader, even wearing a costume with a helmet, just out of spite this time

Â•Said infant villain channeling Hayden Christensen's Darth Vader, culminating with Anakin's loud line "Traitor!"

Â•Kamino, in the form of an incomplete map to find Luke

Â•Torture scene from EpV

Â•Cantina scene (EpIV, EpII). Maz Kanata is reminiscent of Dexter Jettster and his droid WA7, with just a twist of Yoda.

Â•A hero hanging from the wall of a chasm (EpI)

WTF Moments:

Â•Incredible coincidence: Rey, Finn, and BB-8 run away from a First Order airstrike, towards a ship that is promptly and efficiently destroyed by a TIE Fighter's blast. They are forced to run towards a very, very, very old Millennium Falcon and the TIE Fighters become suddenly too incompetent to destroy it. The Falcon is perfectly functional of course, despite having been abandoned for many years. Rey is not just a starving scavenger; she is also the perfect pilot for the Millennium Falcon, defeating trained fighters and pulling incredible stunts the first time she pilots it. Solo and Chewbacca inexplicably find them, just in time to find Luke Skywalker!

Â•A woman that has no idea of what the force is and is too afraid to find out, and according to Joda's standards would be too old to even begin training, is suddenly able to use Jedi mind tricks and is now on the quest to become the best Jedi badass of the galaxy.

Â•The most powerful Sith Lord of the whole galaxy is able to stop energy blasts mid air, kill with the force, read people's minds, and detect subtle tremors in the force like the presence of his non-force-user father from millions of miles away, and is a lightsaber warrior with years of training and experience is somehow the same incompetent guy that is later unable to sense that his father is in the same building, and is later unable to instantly win a lightsaber duel with a guy that had never used a lightsaber before, and then is not only unable to instantly win a lightsaber duel with a woman that had never used a lightsaber before but he is also defeated.

Â•Luke goes into hiding but gives a map with his exact location. Reconstruction is unnecessary, as the small portion contains the names of the star systems. And if it does not, then its position in a complete galactic map can be determined by the sizes of the portion's stars or their spatial configuration.

Â•Once again, the Death Star was destroyed by shots from one single one- manned starfighter.

Â•Finn, an unimportant sanitation stormtrooper among millions of stormtroopers, knows just enough about the First Order in order to destroy its most powerful weapon.

Â•Han Solo, the greatest and most beloved hero of the Star Wars universe dies without a fight, but with a whimper and is then just discarded like a piece of trash.

Â•Now you can go into hyperspace and pass through shields and hulls. This technological advancement is standing right there with Star Trek's superblood and interplanetary teleportation.

Sad, just sad things from this movie:

Â•Zero mystery. I bet the makers tried the concept of having the reveal of Ren as Han and Leia's son to a later part of the movie as a Big Twist, but they realized it wouldn't work and now it comes across as a non-twist. Also, Han's death was totally predictable, and the moment of the end titles was totally predictable.

Â•No villains. Zero complexity. Zero character development. Zero motivation. Forgettable. Who cares about Snoke and Ren?

Â•Star Wars Battlefront, a video game without a plot, feels a lot more like Star Wars than this film.

Â•I can't believe that this film has absolutely zero original ideas. At least the prequels had original ideas despite the fact that everybody knew where were they heading. Oh wait, I was able to find an original idea, that you can go into hyperspace and pass through shields and hulls. Which is a terrible idea.

Â•For this movie's worth of originality, creativity, and action, it might as well have been made by Michael Bay on CGI and digital medium. At least he would bring more explosions to it.

Â•This film played it safe with the designs for new creatures, vehicles, technologies, worlds, costumes. The OT and PT had a lot of creative, inventive, versatile and totally incredible designs.

Â•Suddenly the prequel trilogy doesn't look that bad

Â•Leia was so busy with the resistance that she couldn't make the time to accompany the party that went to see her brother Luke

Â•The next Death Star will surely destroy the entire galaxy

Â•Leia could have been replaced by another character. She was totally inconsequential.

At least this film passes the Bechdel test with two named women.

I think I prefer to dwell in the past. I'll stick to the Old Trilogy.

title: good sci fi movie but an OK star wars movie
review:
After the prequel movies I thought that star wars as a franchise was doomed for the fact that it just flat out sucked. but with this movie I sorta ate my words. Now before i get into detail this review does some mild spoilers. Now let's talk about cast and characters and I honestly have to say they did a good job. Each actor and actress did a good job and overall gave a good performance and i felt that they all were the right choice for the characters. I mainly want to give props to Daisy Ridley, i think that she has a lot of potential and if she just keeps working hard i feel that she could become an amazing actress. I also felt like the new characters that they gave us were really well written and I think that all the time and effort they put into them was well worth it. It was also good how they developed the characters because I thought that this movie had a lot of good character development. I mainly liked how they made it to where the development of the characters was interesting and how mostly everything that happened to the character mattered and had a purpose which overall gave almost each character a decent character arc that I believe will get wider and better as the series goes on. But there was one character that i thought was a waste of potential was captain phasma and the reason why i say that was because we didn't really see much of her which is a mistake because they could have added a complete different side to character and really made her a part of the star wars universe but instead she turned out to be like boba fett unless she is still alive in the next movie.

Speaking of the characters i would also like to talk about the main antagonist Kylo Ren. This character is a great villain because not only will you hate his character as a villain, but you will also understand why he is doing what he is doing and you will understand his motives which throughout multiple examples makes certain villains stand out as great in film and fiction novels alike.

When it came to the plot I think that this is when star wars falls flat on it's face. The reason why I say this i because many points in the plot were copy and paste from the fourth installment which I won't exploit because it would be a long boring list. The reason why i mention this is because even though almost everyone loved A New Hope's plot we didn't ask for a reboot we asked for a sequel. Now yes providing a new story line and content was where the prequel movies fell, but you can't be afraid to try something new and even though it's a good remake we were still (the star wars community) were let down. Another thing i would like to mention is that certain aspects of the plot I felt were rushed. I also noticed that the new Jedi in the series developed her skills not only with a light saber but with the force a little too fast to where it seemed unreasonable when she beat Kylo Ren the first time she ever fought with a light saber and performed the Jedi mind trick only after somewhere around three attempts. Now when it comes to the set I was really impressed with what they did. What really impressed me was the fact that they tried to use CGI as little as possible and when they did it looked really nice and it was good to the point where i didn't really realize it when I was watching. The reason why I'm making this a huge deal is because when I was watching the movie it seemed like everything was real, and it increases the ability to immerse yourself into the movie especially if you saw it in imax 3D. So that's all I have to say I'm sure that I have missed some stuff but i would give this as a 7.5 but i'll be generous and give 8 out of 10 stars.

title: Fun film despite some flaws
review: Star Wars is one of the most established movie series of all time. Despite these films being a tad overrated, I find myself enjoying these films myself. Star Wars: The Force Awakens, was no different. One thing that is overlooked in Star Wars I feel is just how cheesy they can be. That something that I think tons of people glance over when they're watching a Star Wars movie, and the same goes for this one. There was a good handful of cheesy scenes and dialogue that was hard to sit through. While it didn't ruin the movie, it was still quite hard to watch. The action scenes in this film, however, were nice and fluid and well orchestrated, much like the original films. The new characters were fun and interesting and probably the most exciting part of the whole film. Overall, I don't have much to say about The Force Awakens. Yes, it was good, and yes, it was infinitely better than any prequel film. It did have it's pitfalls with some of the dialogue and even some boring scenes, and it for sure felt like a revitalization of the series by bringing back certain key plot elements from the some of the first films. Overall, though, I had fun. That's all that really matters when it comes to Star Wars anyway.

title: New Hope 2.0
review:
The Force Awakens (TFA) returns a major element to the Star Wars franchise; fun.

Daisey Ridley and John Boyega own their characters Rey and Finn respectively. Oscar Isaac's X-Wing pilot Poe is all glorious hero. Adam Driver is absolutely pitch perfect in the role of Kylo Ren. Harrison Ford is more engaged than he has been in a decade. BB8 is the new droid star of the franchise, an absolute marvel of performance and special effects.

The story is very much A New Hope 2.0, which is not a bad thing, but it has been a source of heated debate among fans. There are character and story seeds planted that we do not get to see to fruition by the end credits, or in some cases, require repeated viewings to catch them. This is yet another source of heated debate among fans. I am not sure why it is a bad thing that a movie require you see it multiple times, isn't that the fun of watching movies? This is the first of a trilogy of films and the expectation is those seeds not bloomed will produce fruit in the other two films. It is admittedly a less individually standing film out of all the films in the franchise. However, I have confidence all will be revealed in the coming episodes. John Williams once again adds to the overall experience, though this is the first film that lacks a core musical theme which makes the score rather by the numbers which is a slight disappointment.

A lot of fans have commented there is a sense that the Rey character is a "Mary Sue" of sorts and Finn's character has a turn of conscious that is too quick and without much back-story. Personally I found there is more than enough there that you don't have to be shown every single little thread to justify a character's arc, you should be able to figure out on your own some aspects given what we do know otherwise you are looking at a 3hr bore fest of exposition just because some fans have to have everything spelled out for them. Specific to the Rey character, I find it hypocritical that this character is singled out as too equipped when the fantasy and action genre is filled with beloved MALE characters who are equipped similarly yet accepted without question.

Personally, I really have only two major complaints. The first is that the highly publicized and promoted character Captain Phasma is criminally under utilized in the film, in fact, ultimately reduced to a weak character which is a huge disappointment. My other major issue is how Solo's character arc finale was handled. Solo's arc finale should have been a huge emotional moment, but ends up being rushed through and lacks the emotional gravitas it should have had. The ball was dropped here in a big way.

So, to sum it up, TFA does rely heavily on nostalgia/familiar story elements, it plants some seeds that are yet to bloom, while it does give you enough in some areas you just have to utilize that information to form some of the information on your own. We have one highly promoted character criminally underused and another classic character's arc finale rushed. Still, the fantastic cast, performances, chemistry, action and SFX return the franchise to solid footing and I look forward to the coming episodes.

title: A spectacular return to the Star Wars cinematic universe.
review:
Though I will freely admit that I saw this movie through rose-tinted glasses, I can safely say that The Force Awakens, after two viewings, met all of my expectations. This is a pure action-adventure science fiction film, and its 135 minutes run at an absolute tear from beginning to end, with little quarter given. In short: it is, technically speaking, exactly what the anti-prequel crowd was looking for.

I, for one, do not count myself among that crowd. I grew up with Episodes I-III, so they will always have a place in my heart, even if their flaws have become more and more apparent to me over the years. These flaws (poor dialogue, questionable direction, uneven pacing, awkward romances) have been duly noted by J.J. Abrams. The dialogue in Episode VII isn't award-worthy, but it's efficient and well-spoken. The movie moves between characters and locations seamlessly, maintaining a focused, exciting, yet simple story throughout. In my opinion, all of the actors have really solid chemistry, and I especially look forward to seeing more of the newest characters.

John Boyega fits the young, flawed hero role like a glove. Finn is a very easy guy to like very quickly. I forgot that this was Daisy Ridley's first major motion picture almost immediately; I enjoyed watching Rey learn what she's capable of. I've saved my highest praise for Adam Driver as Kylo Ren, however. He almost never falls short of intimidating, but his very emotional approach to the Dark Side gives him more depth than the screenwriters were obligated to give him. I appreciated this.

I think my complaints primarily centre around certain elements of the film that felt too familiar. There has been widespread talk that the film emulates far too much of previous Star Wars films. I'd say this is perhaps objectively true, but how much it affects your experience really depends on what attitude you go into the movie with. There were a small number of moments where I felt like the production team should have gone for something more original, but it's hard to be too upset when you have a goofy grin on your face for more than two hours.

In the great words of our lord: "I laughed, I cried, I lost ten pounds". I'd tell you to go see this movie, but you already have. I'm excited for what the future will bring for this franchise.

title: Yes, it really is that good
review:
This movie does everything right. Right from the start, I was sucked into the story. It may not have the sort of punch that Mad Max Fury Road had, but there are so many ways this could have gone wrong, and I'm so glad they did it right. Lets first touch upon the main criticism that I've seen about this movie. People say that it follows the structure of the original movie beat for beat. And yes, this is true. However, the movie also does plenty of innovation and world building of its own. And so this movie does feel new, even though it follows the same structure.

The movie pays a lot of homage to the old movies, but not in that annoying Kingdom of the Crystal Skull way. There aren't constant wink winks to the audience. Instead they recognize lots of stuff from the old movies in a loving way. These are the sort of nods to the old movies that feel just right. Stars like Carry Fisher and Harrison Ford aren't just brought back for a cameo, but play an important part in the movie. In fact, Han Solo is one of the main characters throughout the entire movie. Leia's role is decidedly smaller, but still important. I also felt Harrison Ford did a really good job. He really was Han Solo again. Carry Fisher is just okay, but Ford IS Han Solo.

I was afraid that perhaps the new characters would not grow on me, but fortunately that wasn't the case. Finn's role is just perfect, plus it allows the movie to give the audience more insight into the structure of the empire, and what being a Storm Trooper is all about. This is the world building I was talking about earlier. The movie answers a lot of questions, even the simple ones. Rey is also a great character, but the exact opposite of Finn. Plus I really enjoyed the way the movie dispels common damsel in distress tropes with her. It was almost a slightly feminist movie in that sense, but in a good way. I think Rey's character makes the Star Wars universe more accessible to a young female audience, and that thought makes me smile a little. The movie does its best to show us that Rey is perfectly fine at saving herself.

The opening shot of the original Star Wars had its audience literally ducking in their seats, and thus succeeded at making you feel the oppressive rule of the empire with a mere visual. But The Force Awakens nails that too. Rather than steal those shots, they have new shots to achieve the same thing. A lot of the shots of imperial ships are shot at an angle from below, so they look really big.

The special effects in this are also amazing. There is so much use of real sets and practical effects. Tons of creatures are puppets, animatronics, or suit-characters. -Even some of the really big creatures are puppets, I suspect. This makes the world look real. Sure, when it comes to big battle scenes there is also liberal use of CGI. But unlike Age of Ultron, it doesn't look like CGI. It looks like the characters are really there, I also really like the way they show the interior of various ships, and show how the technology works. It makes it all feel real.

Plot wise, the movie succeeds at making the First Order feel threatening, by showing the cruelty of the empire early on. This is something that the old movies never really succeeded at. They always made the Storm Troopers look like bumbling cannon fodder, -but not so in this movie. They also have some fun with the villain, which is welcome. He isn't just some two dimensional character.

Another thing that surprised me, is how they expand on the lore of The Force. We get to see new ways in which the Force can be used, and they focus more on the mystical elements of it, and don't even mention the midichlorians from the prequels. And we get to see the Force being used a lot. If you think about it, Darth Vader didn't use the Force all that much in the original trilogy, and neither did Obi Wan. But in the Force Awakens, we see liberal use of it.

So with this avalanche of praise, is there anything bad about the movie? Yes, but it is only minor. The movie had me along for the majority of it, up until the end. The final part of the movie is where it kind of lost me. And it just didn't blow me away, like Mad Max Fury Road did. It is perhaps unfair to expect a movie to have that much of an impact, because the few times that it has happened, it was always a surprise. But that's not the only problem. The ending just was a bit lacking. It feels like the movie doesn't end on a high note, like the original movies all did. It tries to end on a cliff hanger, but it doesn't really work. And perhaps the predictability of the ending is to blame for that. I also felt some of the villains were a bit silly. Kylo Ren is just fine. But some of the others are a bit goofy (and they have goofy names too).

If you have children you owe it to them to take them to this movie. I mean it. Take them to this movie right now! They will love you for it! Come on! Reserve those tickets already. And if you are still a child at heart, then go see it as well.

title: The Force is back, but is it for real?
review:
I've been digesting JJ Abrams' much anticipated, and by now highly praised, take on Star Wars for the last four hours, trying to reconcile the thoughts spinning around in my head. I sense now that it'll be some time - likely after another viewing - before I really know what I think about it. For now, as sheer popcorn entertainment, it may be unmatched by anything I've seen as an adult. Certainly in this millennium. And armed with distinct advantages such as emotional and narrative track already laid and a huge well of nostalgia, which it mines at times both expertly and overtly, it certainly packs a punch beyond the cheap thrills we often associate with modern blockbusters.

But the question that still hangs over me now is "Is it Star Wars, or merely a very good imitation?", because at times this felt like attending a concert from your favorite band only to discover that it's merely a very good tribute band. I don't say that because of its lack of originality (a crime of which it is most certainly guilty), but because it very much feels like someone else playing a familiar tune, if that makes any sense. Make no mistake, 'The Force Awakens' looks, sounds and behaves more like the original trilogy than the prequels ever did, but where the latter felt merely like new (and certainly lesser in my opinion) material from the same artist, this feels like an interpretation of existing material, which of course it is. JJ Abrams directs the film in the same way someone who grew up listening to Eddie Van Halen would play the guitar, but not exactly like Eddie Van Halen himself.

There is much to like here. Actual locations, real men inside real Stormtrooper costumes, many practical alien creatures. They do make a difference. There's plenty of CGI, and the bulk of it is exceptional, but I felt a greater investment here because so much care had been taken to ground it in a tangible reality. The performances are also quite good. Certainly the script is better than those of the PT (though its far from perfect), which helps, as does the aforementioned "reality" in my opinion, but Abrams and Co. did a good job selecting this cast. I wasn't just marking time when a recognizable face wasn't on screen. I instantly liked these characters, both in conception and execution. I feel they're strong enough to carry this new story going forward, and I'm anxious to see their evolution. But the star of this movie is, without question, Harrison Ford as Han Solo. He's everything you could've hoped for, and much more. I can't remember the last time I saw Ford so invested in a role. He's the Han Solo we all remember and love. A little slower, certainly grayer, but with the same lopsided grin and unshakable confidence. He has a nice touch of pathos here, but he wears it like a hat, not a wet cloak.

As I said, it'll be some time before I really know how I feel about 'The Force Awakens'. What I know for sure is that it moved me to tears more than once, gave me goose bumps and made me cheer and applaud enthusiastically on several occasions, and that's more than I can say about the prequels.

title: The Force is strong with this one
review: I am and old Star Wars fan and this time I was not disappointed. After the sad experience of the prequels, I felt back in the same spirit that made the original trilogy so great. JJ Abrams managed the material with great respect and put a particular attention in creating a proper continuity with the first movies. I was particularly impressed by how the environment and the technology look the same. For example, the holograms you will see on the Tie Fighters, the X wings or the Command centre look exactly like the ones that were available with the '70s and 80's cinematography. The script is good and leaves several subplots open for the future developments. It is true, as some commenters have already reported, that the TFA "homages" to the previous stories can create a feeling of quasi-remake as done in "Jurassic World". My personal feeling is that while in a couple of cases some coincidences were too forced, the repetition of the events is in the logic of SW universe and in the Force balance as was heavily suggested in ROTJ.

title: I didn't want this movie to be bad but,
review:
It is bad. Sorry everybody. The excellent CGI is pretty much the only thing positive about The Force Awakens.

There are plenty of other reviewers that have explained why this is a bad movie already, but what I can't explain is why professional critics have either remained silent or given this a good review.

This movie has the kind of script you would expect a failing liberal arts student to submit. It makes EVERY mistake that an amateur screenwriter would make. It's so unoriginal and there's so much Deus Ex Machina I don't know where to start.

I don't want to ruin the plot, but you've already seen this movie before if you've seen episode IV so I almost can't. The writing really is that lazy.

Except episode IV was better. There are so many things in The Force Awakens that don't make sense if you pay attention. The action simply progresses without reason or purpose. The entire conflict is built on the paper-thin foundations. And there are no character motivations, good or bad, that are explained or justified in any way. Again, lazy writing.

The bad guys' main weapon is just silly, hopelessly expensive and impractical (e.g. it can't move), and poorly thought-out (just like this movie). And the good guys' response to it is equally silly, making the main conflict a joke.

The nail in the coffin is how conveniently and effortlessly.. and inexplicably.. the conflict is resolved at the end. There may as well have been text flashing across the screen about two-thirds through the movie, "then all the problems were solved. The End..."

At least that wouldn't have wasted the audience's time, because the actual ending was almost just as lazy.

Honestly, only reason I can see that the script made it past the trash can is because it had Star Wars on the cover. If this were ANY other movie no one would have even looked at it. This movie will not age well. Try re-watching this in ten years after the hype has died down and see if the good reviews hold up. I think they won't.

This is probably the most bloated, expensive, B-movie ever made. Deus Ex Machina is a classic symptom of bad screen writing, and it happens a lot in The Force Awakens. Any professional critic knows this and should pick up on it immediately. So, why was a movie with this many problems and no originality, SO well received by critics?

title: Predictable, full of plot holes, But nevertheless: A whole lot of fun!!
review:
The Force Awakens is mostly a rehash of ANH with some ESB and ROTJ thrown in the mix. It has plenty of plot holes you can easily fly the falcon trough, but is so much damn fun nonetheless an just what someone who loved Star Wars as a kid wants to see after 30 years. Yes I've grown up and like other films better, but I didn't expect another Empire compared to A New Hope. And if you don't also you will not be disappointed.

If you love Star Wars, you'll love this. Plenty of moments which reminiscent events form the original trilogy and we get to see Han Solo back in action.

Yes, blow up another shield generator and yes, destroy another super weapon, but isn't that what we came to see? I did.

JJ made a great homage to the original trilogy and it looks like a great starting point to go from for episodes 8 and 9.

title: Welcome Again
review:
I watched the movie a few hours ago, I was not expecting so much before I went to cinema, but to my surprise it made me feel like I was watching original star wars trilogy. I mean it took me to my teenage and I enjoyed it so much.

title: Tremendously entertaining regardless of the slightly derivative plot
review:
First of all I am only writing this review in response to seeing some hugely unfair critiques on this website. Every film has flaws but to label The Force Awakens a 4 star film (0.6 above the average rating for Jack and Jill) is beyond harsh. In general criticism appears to revolve around

1) Being too similar to Episode IV 2) Having a weak Villain that is too conveniently beaten 3) Captain Phasma being barely developed 4) Rei and Finn being childish and detracting from the emotional tension of the film 5) A lack of explanation of the events between VI and VII mostly relating to the First Order 6) The score not matching the quality of the other films

Whilst these criticisms are valid to varying degrees, the casting, dialogue and pacing allow you to enjoy the film if you allow yourself to. I feel there was a good balance between developing characters and action sequences aligning the film more closely with what made the original trilogy so immersive as opposed to the CGI indulgent prequels. To address the criticisms specifically:

1) Perhaps the most valid criticism, you cannot deny the comparison of the plot to a new hope. At times this borders on being obvious enough to divert attention away from what is happening so I will accept that the plot is not hugely original. However, the same story is told in an original way with a different tone. Also it's not as if it's a bad plot anyway and the film was always in danger of falling into the trap of a Hollywood blockbuster in being creatively stifled in order to appeal to a mass audience. Despite this problem, the execution is good enough to overcome the issue. Furthermore it is important to appreciate this is the first act of a three act structure and sets up plenty of plot threads to develop that are distinct from episode IV. Hopefully this film will appear less derivative when viewed in the context of the trilogy as a whole

2) This criticism misses the point of the character. Kylo Ren is a young poorly trained Sith who clearly has major issues with what he has to do to fulfill his perceived destiny. The entire point is he fails miserably to live up to his idol in almost every aspect. He makes a lot of strategic errors, is easily beaten by someone only just discovering her power and has nowhere near the prestige within the first order that Darth Vader had in the empire despite his best efforts. Does this make him a weak villain, of course, but that is the idea. Across the rest of the films I would expect him to become far stronger and more ruthless thus this film is really just the start of the characters development into hopefully a villain with great depth. Of course this is all dependent on the other films so this criticism could either become more or less valid over time

3) Fair play she hardly did anything. I would make the point again that she should become more relevant in the next film but you wouldn't lose much from cutting her character in this film on it's own. Perhaps as a general note, there may be too many characters so this issue is an inevitable consequence.

4) This is very unfair as they set the tone of the film. It has an underlying levity throughout, largely down to the comic chemistry between Boyega and Ridley. Perhaps they are childish at times but this is the start of their journey so this apparent naivety must be viewed in the context of the trilogy. When there are dramatic moments in the plot however, I feel they react appropriately and actually add to it. I feel like they have a great deal of on screen chemistry and Boyega in particularly has natural comedic ability which is far more understated than other blockbuster actors. One criticism that I find utterly absurd is that casting Rei was "to have a female protagonist, Yay feminism" or casting Finn was"to have a black protagonist, yay affirmative action". They are cast because they perform the roles well together and gender or race is an irrelevance. The black stormtrooper controversy is also ridiculous as Abrams clearly realised the major issue with stormtroopers as clones means you don't care about them and challenging the clones idea will ultimately make the conflict more meaningful

5) The film was long enough as it is. Perhaps they tried to cover too much ground but hopefully the first order will be more developed in subsequent films. To be fair, The origin of the empire is not really explained in a new hope and that doesn't seem to bother fans too much.

6) John Williams is probably my favourite film composer because of his ability to come up with such iconic themes and motifs and orchestrate them so creatively. The importance of music in star wars is often under appreciated and whilst the themes are not as iconic as the imperial march for example, they are well written and permeate the score more than you initially realise. I expect that in the future, people will come to appreciate Rei's theme, The resistance march and Jedi Steps as iconic despite how initially forgetful they are. Whilst I was initially underwhelmed, it improves on repeat exposure so don't dismiss it too quickly.

As discussed there is some validity to each of these criticisms yet overall, I feel that the film is well cast, well scripted, doesn't overuse action scenes at the expense of character/plot development and is fundamentally emotionally engaging, restoring what was so beloved about the original trilogy and what was sorely lacking in episodes I-III.

title: Amazing? Not quite, but it is VERY good.
review:
First of all, there's a lot of whiny, know-nothing, 'think-they're-fan-boy' nonsense written on here, that is to the word 'Review' what Bieber is to 'Music'. Take the hostile responses and the gleeful 'Its amazing!!' gush out of here, and what you're left with is probably quite accurate.. Overall, Id give it a solid 8/10. The introduction of the new characters is very good. They're rounded characters; Finn came across as funny, but not entirely likable, which was interesting. Not your indentikit 'hero'. Rey on the other hand is likable, and it was quite easy to find yourself rooting for her in much the same way you did for Luke Skywalker originally. By the end of the film, enough of her story is missing to suggest that the next couple of films will reveal a lot more of interest about her. Kylo Ren proved to be different kind of bad guy - some will criticise him for being tantrum -prone, but this is no Anakin of the prequels - he is plenty ruthless and sinister when he wants to be. It would also have been too easy to make him a facsimile of an iconic villain like Vader. Some media have suggested he could be more iconic than Vader - I wouldn't go that far, but he's definitely promising, and certainly a worthy villain to rank alongside Maul, Dooku, and the rest.

The whole film is stolen by Harrison Ford. Don't be fooled by the trailer, his role isn't just to provide 'nostalgia'. He's a major player, and he brings humour, tetchiness, intelligence and pathos to the role all at once. You always get the impression in interviews that Ford really doesn't enjoy playing the part; if that's true, you'd never know it.

Happily, Carrie Fisher was much better than I was expecting, given that she's not exactly a prolific actress. The partnership with Ford seemed to click instantly into gear. Oscar Isaac is enjoyable as Poe Dameron, although I felt of all the characters, his was the one that went slightly underdeveloped.

The cinematography is excellent - the Millennium Falcon, Tie Fighters, X-Wings, etc. never looked so crisp and vivid - the 3D was also well done, and the effects, as ever are excellent. Aliens looked real, battle scenes looked epic, nothing looked digital - except perhaps Snoke, but that is because he appears as a hologram.

If I had some criticisms, it would be that the story perhaps followed that of A New Hope a little too closely - some elements have been turned on their head, but essentially, its a similar film. I can see why it was written this way, but at times it felt just a little too familiar to the previous stories.

I was also a bit disappointed with John Williams score. The music that was composed for the trailers is superior by a long distance. For the film, there are the familiar thematic cues for the force, and Han and Leia, but other than that nothing stood out. Neither Finn, Rey nor Ren are given a particularly strong or memorable musical cue, and even the music accompanying the battle scenes is average. I was somewhat disappointed and I'd go as far as saying its the weakest soundtrack of all the Star Wars films.

One thing I noticed that I did think was interesting though... well, I thought so anyway... is that I'm pretty sure its the first Star Wars film that explicitly shows blood. Further evidence of the new direction, perhaps.

So in summary, very good, a really enjoyable return to form for Star Wars - bit it doesn't knock The Empire Strikes Back off its perch!

title: Awesome Movie
review: I have seen Star Wars in 1977 and since then I have seen all the episodes muliple times. The force awakens is one of the best entries in the series if not the best one yet. I do not understand any negative reviews especially by the so called original fans. This movie is awesome and outstanding. Kylo Ren is the best Star Wars villain yet. Yes, he is whiny, jeaulous, insecure and weak but that is what makes him so dangerous and unexplainable. The young actors are by far better than Hamill, Ford and Fisher were in 1977. Especially Daisy Ridley does a very good and very convincing job. By the way the movie is set to entertain and that is what it does perfectly so. 10/10 for sure!

title: I have felt the Force !
review:
The Force Awakens was an amazing star wars movie . Its the beginning of a new chapter . Its how all beginnings are . After the movie ended i wanted more and there are more episodes coming soon ! I agree that the movie had a few unanswered questions but it is absolutely worth to wait for them to be answered . Its like when A New Hope released in 1977 , many answers were not told like who Darth Vader was or why does he always wear a mask etc . People were left on a cliffhanger after watching it and had to wait 3 years for the Empire Strikes Back to release which answered many questions .

Its the same as in The Force Awakens . It wasn't possible for J.J Adrams to answer all the questions for the people . Wheres the fun in that ? Most movie critics will look at the 'flaws' in the movie but come on very movie has flaws even the greatest ones .
